rows.question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).

rows.question: Does the obligation to indicate that deep-fakes are artificially generated apply when prosecuting a criminal offence?
rows.answer: No. Under Article 50(4), the deployer's duty to disclose that image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake has been artificially generated or manipulated does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute criminal offences. Absent that law-enforcement authorisation, the deployer must disclose that the content is a deep fake.

rows.question: When the intended use of an AI system is listed in Annex III of the EU AI Act, the AI system is automatically high-risk, isn't it? If not, can you explain when that is not the case?
rows.answer: No. An AI system used for a purpose listed in Annex III is not automatically high-risk. Article 6(2) sets the default rule that Annex III systems "shall be considered to be high-risk", but Article 6(3) creates an exception. The Article 6(3) exception. An Annex III system is not high-risk if it "does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making." The exception applies only where at least one of these conditions is met. (a) the system is intended to perform a narrow procedural task; (b) the system is intended to improve the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) the system is intended to detect decision-making patterns, or deviations from earlier patterns, and is not meant to replace or influence the previous human assessment without proper human review; (d) the system is intended to perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use case. Profiling always makes the system high-risk. Under the last subparagraph of Article 6(3), an Annex III system that profiles natural persons "shall always be considered to be high-risk." In that case the exception cannot apply, even if one of conditions (a) to (d) is met. What the provider must still do. Under Article 6(4), a provider that considers its Annex III system not high-risk must document that assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service. It must provide that documentation to national competent authorities if they ask for it. The provider must also still register itself and the system in the EU database under Article 49(2). Articles 6(5) to 6(8) add the following. The Commission must issue guidelines with practical examples of high-risk and non-high-risk use cases. The Commission may adopt delegated acts to add, change or remove the Article 6(3) conditions. Any such change must not lower the overall level of protection the Regulation provides. Some systems are outside Annex III in the first place. Some Annex III entries are limited by their own wording, so a system may not be covered by the entry at all. For example. Point 1 (biometrics) and point 6 (law enforcement) apply only "in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law.". Point 1(a) excludes biometric verification whose sole purpose is to confirm that a person is who they claim to be. Point 5(b) excludes AI systems used to detect financial fraud. A system outside these entries never needs the Article 6(3) exception, because Article 6(2) never applied to it.

rows.question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
rows.answer: No, the AI system is not "medium risk." It is a high-risk AI system under Article 6(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. Why "medium risk" doesn't carry over. The AI Act has no "medium risk" category. The "medium-risk" label comes from the medical device classification rules, which grade devices by risk. The AI Act does not reuse those grades. It uses its own test in Article 6. Why the AI system is high-risk. Under Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk when both of these conditions are met. The AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I. Medical devices are covered by Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (Annex I, point 11), and in vitro diagnostic devices by Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (Annex I, point 12). The operator's AI system is a safety component of a medical device, so this condition is met. That product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under the Annex I legislation before it is placed on the market or put into service. The operator's device goes through a notified-body assessment, so this condition is met too. Two further points follow from the wording of the Act. The device's class doesn't matter. Once the device needs a third-party assessment, it makes no difference whether it is low, medium or high risk under the device rules. Being in a medium-risk class matters only because that class requires a notified body. Selling the AI system separately doesn't change this. Article 6(1) applies "irrespective of whether" the AI system is placed on the market or put into service on its own. The Article 6(3) exception does not apply. Article 6(3) lets some systems avoid high-risk status: those that pose no significant risk of harm and perform only a narrow procedural task, improve the result of a completed human activity, detect decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing human assessment, or perform a preparatory task. That exception covers only Annex III systems under Article 6(2), not systems that are high-risk through the Annex I product route. What this means in practice. Requirements: the AI system must meet the high-risk requirements in Chapter III, Section 2 (Article 8). These include a risk management system (Article 9), data governance (Article 10) and transparency to deployers (Article 13). Conformity assessment: under Article 43(3), you follow the conformity assessment procedure already required under the medical device legislation, and the Section 2 requirements become part of it. Annex VII points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 also apply. This lets the notified body access training, validation and test data, require further tests, access the trained models where necessary, and refuse a certificate on data-quality grounds, which then requires re-training. The operator's medical device notified body may check the AI requirements if its compliance with Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11) was assessed when it was notified. Documentation: under Article 8(2), you may fold the AI Act testing, reporting and documentation into the documentation and procedures you already maintain for the device. For example, the Article 9 risk management can sit alongside the operator's ISO 14971 process. Future changes: if you substantially modify the AI system, it needs a new conformity assessment (Article 43(4)). Changes you pre-determined and recorded in the technical documentation for a system that keeps learning are not treated as substantial modifications.

Condition (b): that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment

rows.question: Does the EU AI Act explicitly requires to use explainable AI techniques such as LIME or SHAP to increase the trustworthiness of high-risk AI systems?
rows.answer: No, the EU AI Act mandates no specific explainable-AI technique such as LIME or SHAP, and Article 13 instead requires only that high-risk AI systems be sufficiently transparent for deployers to interpret their output. Article 14 requires effective human oversight, and Article 15 requires appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. The Act is technique-agnostic, so the choice of any interpretability method is left to the provider.

rows.question: Does the EU AI Act apply to AI systems or AI models or both?
rows.answer: Article 2(1)(a) covers providers placing AI systems on the Union market or putting them into service, and providers placing general-purpose AI models on the market, irrespective of where the providers are established. AI systems are defined in Article 3(1), while general-purpose AI models are regulated separately under Chapter V (Articles 51 to 56), are defined in Article 3(63), and carry their own provider obligations with additional duties for models posing systemic risk.

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.answer: No, the system is not prohibited. It is also not high-risk under Annex III, because Annex III expressly excludes biometric verification whose sole purpose is to confirm that a specific person is who they claim to be. Article 5(1) lists the banned practices, and a one-to-one identity check does not match any of them. Article 5(1)(h) bans only the use of "real-time" remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, subject to the exceptions in points (h)(i) to (iii). Confirming a claimed identity is not remote biometric identification. Article 5(1)(g) bans biometric categorisation that infers race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. Pure verification infers none of these. Article 5(1)(f) bans inferring emotions in the workplace or in education, except for medical or safety reasons. Verification does not infer emotions. Article 5(1)(e) bans untargeted scraping of facial images to build or expand facial recognition databases. Verification does not require this. Article 5(1)(a) to (d) cover manipulation, exploiting vulnerabilities, social scoring and predictive policing based solely on profiling. None of these applies to confirming a claimed identity. Annex III, point 1(a), lists remote biometric identification systems but adds: "This shall not include AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be." the operator's system therefore does not fall within Article 6(2). Since it is not an Annex III system, the Article 6(3) derogation test does not come into play. Limits on that conclusion. Sole purpose. The exclusion only covers verification. If the system also searches a database to identify people (one-to-many matching), it becomes an Annex III, point 1(a), system. Depending on its use, Article 5(1)(h) could then apply. Other biometric uses. If the system also categorises people by sensitive or protected attributes (Annex III, point 1(b)) or recognises emotions (Annex III, point 1(c)), it becomes high-risk. Inferring the attributes listed in Article 5(1)(g) is prohibited outright. Product route. Under Article 6(1), the system is still high-risk if it is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I law (or is itself such a product) and that product needs a third-party conformity assessment. The Annex III exclusion does not change this. Transparency. Article 50(3) requires deployers to inform people only for emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems, so it does not apply here. If the system interacts directly with people, Article 50(1) requires the provider to design it so they are told they are dealing with an AI system. That duty does not apply where this is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, or to systems authorised by law to fight crime. Under Article 50(5), the information must be clear and given no later than the first interaction. The processing of biometric data is still governed by Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (the GDPR).

rows.question: Are AI safety components within medical devices of MDR class IIa, IIb, or III considered to be high-risk according to the EU AI Act? Why?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI system used as a safety component of a medical device in MDR class IIa, IIb or III is high-risk under Article 6(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. Article 6(1) sets two conditions, and both must be met. The AI system must be intended as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I. The same applies where the AI system is itself such a product. Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices is listed in Annex I, point 11, so this condition is met. It also covers AI that qualifies as a medical device in its own right. The product must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that Annex I legislation before it is placed on the market or put into service. Under the MDR, class IIa, IIb and III devices must be assessed with a notified body. That third-party requirement is what meets this condition. This applies whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service with the device or separately. Class I devices that the MDR lets the manufacturer self-certify fail condition (b), so this route would not make their AI high-risk. The Annex III derogation does not apply. Article 6(3) lets a provider show that a system is not high-risk because it poses no significant risk, for example because it only performs a narrow procedural task. That derogation is expressly "by derogation from paragraph 2", so it only covers Annex III use cases. It cannot remove high-risk status gained under Article 6(1). For the same reason, the duty in Article 6(4) to document a "not high-risk" assessment and register the system does not arise. Conformity assessment under Article 43(3). The provider follows the MDR's own conformity assessment procedure. It does not use the Annex III procedures in Article 43(1) and (2). Within that procedure. The requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 apply and form part of the MDR assessment. Points 4.3, 4.4 and 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also apply. Notified bodies designated under the MDR may check the AI system against Section 2. This is allowed only if their notification procedure assessed them against Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11). Some sectoral laws let a manufacturer opt out of third-party assessment by applying harmonised standards. The manufacturer may use that option only if it also applies harmonised standards or common specifications covering all Section 2 requirements. For MDR class IIa, IIb and III devices, notified body involvement remains required. Later changes (Article 43(4)). A substantial modification requires a new conformity assessment. For systems that keep learning after being placed on the market, changes the provider pre-determined at the initial assessment are not a substantial modification. Those changes must be documented in the technical documentation under point 2(f) of Annex IV.

rows.question: What documentation does a provider of a high-risk AI system needs to keep available for the national competent authorities, and for how long?
rows.answer: Under Article 18, for ten years after the high-risk AI system is placed on the market or put into service, the provider must keep at the disposal of the national competent authorities the technical documentation (Article 11), the quality-management-system documentation (Article 17), the documentation of any changes approved by notified bodies, the decisions and other documents issued by notified bodies, and the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47). Separately, under Article 19 the automatically generated logs must be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose, of at least six months.

rows.question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
rows.answer: Article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 governs human oversight measures. It applies to high-risk AI systems. The core duty (Article 14(1)): High-risk AI systems must be designed and developed, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, so that natural persons can effectively oversee them while they are in use. The aim (Article 14(2)): Oversight must aim to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety or fundamental rights. This covers use in line with the intended purpose and reasonably foreseeable misuse. It matters most where such risks remain despite the other requirements of that Section. The type of measures (Article 14(3)): Measures must be commensurate with the system's risks, level of autonomy and context of use. They can take one or both of these forms. Measures the provider identifies and, where technically feasible, builds into the system before it is placed on the market or put into service (point (a)); measures the provider identifies before that point as appropriate for the deployer to implement (point (b)). What the assigned persons must be able to do (Article 14(4)): The system must be provided to the deployer so that the natural persons assigned to oversight can, as appropriate and proportionate. (a) understand the system's relevant capacities and limitations, and monitor its operation, including detecting and addressing anomalies, dysfunctions and unexpected performance; (b) stay aware of automation bias, meaning the tendency to rely or over-rely on the output, especially where the system provides information or recommendations for decisions by natural persons; (c) correctly interpret the output, for example using the available interpretation tools and methods; (d) decide in any particular situation not to use the system, or to disregard, override or reverse its output; (e) intervene in its operation, or interrupt it through a "stop" button or similar procedure that brings it to a halt in a safe state. Remote biometric identification (Article 14(5)): This applies to systems under Annex III, point 1(a). The deployer must take no action or decision based on an identification from the system unless at least two natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority have separately verified and confirmed it. This two-person rule does not apply to such systems used for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum, where Union or national law considers it disproportionate.

rows.question: What is the meaning and purpose of 'testing data' in the context of AI systems, and why is it important that it is not leaked during the training process?
rows.answer: Testing data is one of the training, validation and testing data sets required by Article 10(1); under Article 3(32) it provides an independent evaluation of the system to confirm its expected performance against the intended purpose, after training and validation and before the system is placed on the market. Under Article 10(3) those sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose, with the appropriate statistical properties. If training data leaks into the testing set, the set loses that independence: it can no longer verify Article 10(3) compliance and instead yields inflated, misleading accuracy that masks errors, biases and gaps.

rows.question: What are the high-risk uses of AI systems listed under 'Administration of justice and democratic processes' cited in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Annex III point 8 lists two high-risk use cases under administration of justice and democratic processes. Annex III point 8(a) covers AI systems intended to be used by a judicial authority, or on its behalf, to assist in researching and interpreting facts and the law and in applying the law to a concrete set of facts, or to be used similarly in alternative dispute resolution. Annex III point 8(b) covers AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum, or the voting behaviour of natural persons in exercising their vote, with a carve-out for tools that only organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view.

rows.question: Under what conditions should providers of general-purpose AI models be subject to exceptions regarding transparency-related requirements, if any? And what do those exceptions not cover?
rows.answer: The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.

rows.question: Which AI systems used in education or vocational training should be classified as high-risk according to the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Under Article 6(2) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, an AI system used in education or vocational training is high-risk if it falls within one of the four use cases listed in Annex III, point 3. Each use case applies to educational and vocational training institutions at all levels. Access and admission (Annex III, point 3(a)): systems intended to determine access or admission, or to assign natural persons to such institutions. Evaluating learning outcomes (point 3(b)): systems intended to evaluate learning outcomes, including when those outcomes are used to steer a person's learning process. Level of education (point 3(c)): systems intended to assess the appropriate level of education that an individual will receive or will be able to access, in the context of or within such institutions. Monitoring during tests (point 3(d)): systems intended to monitor and detect prohibited behaviour of students during tests, in the context of or within such institutions. The classification depends on the system's intended purpose. An education tool that does not match one of these four uses is not high-risk under Annex III, point 3. Article 6(3) creates an exception. A system listed in Annex III, point 3 is not high-risk if it poses no significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making. The exception applies only where one of these conditions is met. (a) the system is intended to perform a narrow procedural task; (b) it is intended to improve the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) it is intended to detect decision-making patterns, or deviations from earlier patterns, and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or. (d) it is intended to perform a preparatory task for an assessment relevant to the Annex III use cases. Under the final subparagraph of Article 6(3), a system that profiles natural persons is always high-risk, so the exception is not available to it. Under Article 6(4), a provider relying on the exception must document its assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service. That provider remains subject to the registration obligation in Article 49(2) and must hand over the documentation if national competent authorities request it. There is also a separate product route under Article 6(1). An education-related AI system is high-risk if both of these conditions are met. It is a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the EU product legislation listed in Annex I (for example, the Toys Directive 2009/48/EC in Annex I, point 2). That product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. The Article 6(3) exception does not apply to this product route.

rows.question: What obligations, if any, does the EU AI Act set in place for AI systems that interact directly with natural persons? What exceptions, if any, apply?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 50(1), providers of AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons must design and develop them so that the people concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system. The duty sits with the provider and is built into the system's design. It applies whether or not the system is high-risk. How the information must be given: Under Article 50(5), it must be given to the people concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner, at the latest at the time of the first interaction. It must also meet the applicable accessibility requirements. Exceptions: Article 50(1) contains two. Obvious from context: No disclosure is needed where it is obvious that the person is dealing with an AI system. This is judged from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use. Criminal-law systems: The duty does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. Appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties must still be in place. This exception is lost where the system is available for the public to report a criminal offence, so such a system must still disclose that it is an AI system. Effect on other rules: Under Article 50(6), this transparency duty does not affect the requirements and obligations for high-risk AI systems in Chapter III. It is also without prejudice to other transparency obligations for deployers under Union or national law. A conversational system that is also high-risk, or that also falls within another rule, must meet those obligations as well.

rows.question: What are the administrative fines for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices?
rows.answer: Breaching the Article 5 bans on AI practices can lead to administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000. If the offender is an undertaking, the ceiling is instead up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever amount is higher (Article 99(3)). This is the highest fine level in the Regulation. It covers all eight practices banned under Article 5(1), points (a) to (h). Lower levels apply to other breaches: EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % for the operator and notified-body duties listed in Article 99(4), and EUR 7 500 000 or 1 % for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information under Article 99(5). For SMEs, including start-ups, the ceiling is the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount, not the higher (Article 99(6)). The Member States set the actual penalty rules and must make sure they are enforced. Penalties must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive, and must take into account the interests of SMEs, including start-ups, and their economic viability (Article 99(1)). When deciding whether to fine and how much, authorities must consider all relevant circumstances of the case and, as appropriate (Article 99(7)). (a) the nature, gravity, duration and consequences of the infringement, including the system's purpose, the number of people affected and the level of damage; (b) whether other market surveillance authorities have already fined the same operator for the same infringement; (c) whether other authorities have already fined the same operator for breaches of other Union or national law arising from the same activity; (d) the operator's size, annual turnover and market share; (e) any other aggravating or mitigating factor, such as financial benefits gained or losses avoided; (f) how far the operator cooperated with the national competent authorities; (g) the operator's degree of responsibility, given its technical and organisational measures; (h) how the infringement came to light, in particular whether the operator reported it; (i) whether the infringement was intentional or negligent; (j) any action the operator took to reduce the harm to affected persons. Each Member State decides whether, and how far, public authorities and bodies set up in that State can be fined (Article 99(8)). Where a national legal system has no administrative fines, a competent national court may impose them instead (Article 99(9)). Using these powers is subject to procedural safeguards under Union and national law, including effective judicial remedies and due process (Article 99(10)).

rows.question: How does Annex II relate to prohibited uses of AI systems?
rows.answer: Annex II does not list prohibited practices. It sets the outer limit of one exception to the prohibition in Article 5(1)(h) on using "real-time" remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement. Such use is prohibited unless it is strictly necessary for one of three exhaustive objectives. Only the third objective, in Article 5(1)(h)(iii), relies on Annex II. It covers locating or identifying a person suspected of a criminal offence, for a criminal investigation, a prosecution or the execution of a criminal penalty. The offence must be listed in Annex II and must carry, in the Member State concerned, a custodial sentence or detention order with a maximum period of at least four years. The other two objectives do not depend on Annex II. They are the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation, and for missing persons (point (h)(i)). They also cover preventing a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, or a genuine and present or foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack (point (h)(ii)). Annex II has no bearing on the prohibitions in Article 5(1)(a) to (g). The Annex II list is exhaustive. Terrorism. Trafficking in human beings. Sexual exploitation of children, and child pornography. Illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances. Illicit trafficking in weapons, munitions or explosives. Murder, grievous bodily injury. Illicit trade in human organs or tissue. Illicit trafficking in nuclear or radioactive materials. Kidnapping, illegal restraint or hostage-taking. Crimes within the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court. Unlawful seizure of aircraft or ships. Environmental crime. Organised or armed robbery. Sabotage. Participation in a criminal organisation involved in one or more of these offences. A suspected Annex II offence is necessary but not sufficient. The following conditions also apply. Purpose and safeguards (Article 5(2)): The system may be used only to confirm the identity of the specifically targeted individual. Its use must weigh the seriousness, probability and scale of the harm if the system is not used, against the consequences for the rights and freedoms of everyone affected. It must also respect the safeguards and the time, place and personal limits set by the national law that authorises it. Impact assessment and registration (Article 5(2)): The law enforcement authority must have completed a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and registered the system in the EU database under Article 49. In duly justified cases of urgency, use may start before registration, provided registration is completed without undue delay. Prior authorisation (Article 5(3)): Each use needs prior authorisation from a judicial authority, or from an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding, in the Member State where the use takes place. The authorisation must be issued on a reasoned request and granted only if the use is necessary and proportionate, and limited to what is strictly necessary in time, geography and persons. In a duly justified urgency, use may start without authorisation, but authorisation must be requested without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours. If authorisation is refused, use must stop immediately and all data, results and outputs must be discarded and deleted. No decision with an adverse legal effect on a person may be based solely on the system's output. Notification (Article 5(4)): Each use must be notified to the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority, without sensitive operational data. National law (Article 5(5)): The exception only applies if a Member State chooses to allow it, fully or partially, in national law. That law must set out the rules on authorisation and specify which objectives, including which Annex II offences, may justify use. Member States may also adopt more restrictive rules. Finally, under Article 5(8), meeting these conditions does not override prohibitions that apply because a practice infringes other Union law.

rows.question: Can the European Commission amend Annex III of the EU AI Act to add or modify use-cases classified as high-risk AI systems? Under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes. The Commission can amend Annex III by delegated act to add or modify high-risk use-cases, but only within the limits of Article 7(1) and the procedure in Article 97. Conditions for adding or modifying a use-case. Under Article 7(1), both of the following must be met. (a) Existing area: the AI systems are intended to be used in one of the areas already listed in Annex III. (b) Equivalent or greater risk: the systems pose a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights, that is equivalent to or greater than the risk posed by the high-risk systems already in Annex III. Neither condition is enough on its own. Because of limb (a), the Commission can only add or change use-cases under the eight existing numbered areas. It cannot create a new area this way. How the risk in limb (b) is assessed. Article 7(2) requires the Commission to take into account. (a) the system's intended purpose; (b) how far the system has been used or is likely to be used; (c) the nature and amount of data processed, especially whether special categories of personal data are involved; (d) how autonomously the system acts, and whether a human can override decisions or recommendations that may cause harm; (e) how far its use has already caused harm or adverse impact, or raised significant concerns about it, for example through reports or documented allegations submitted to national competent authorities; (f) the potential extent of the harm, especially its intensity and whether it can affect many people or hit a particular group disproportionately; (g) how dependent affected persons are on the system's outcome, especially where they cannot reasonably opt out for practical or legal reasons; (h) any imbalance of power, or the vulnerability of affected persons relative to the deployer, due to status, authority, knowledge, economic or social circumstances, or age; (i) how easily the outcome can be corrected or reversed; outcomes with an adverse impact on health, safety or fundamental rights are not considered easily correctable or reversible; (j) how large and likely the benefits of deployment are for individuals, groups or society, including possible improvements in product safety; (k) how far existing Union law provides (i) effective redress for the risks, excluding claims for damages, and (ii) effective measures to prevent or substantially minimise those risks. Removing a use-case. Under Article 7(3), the Commission can also remove high-risk systems from Annex III, again only if both conditions are met. (a) the system no longer poses any significant risks to fundamental rights, health or safety, judged against the Article 7(2) criteria; and. (b) the removal does not lower the overall level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights under Union law. Procedure under Article 97. Duration: the power under Article 7(1) and (3) is conferred for five years from 1 August 2024. It is tacitly extended for further five-year periods unless the European Parliament or the Council objects at least three months before a period ends. The Commission must report on the delegation at least nine months before the end of the five-year period (Article 97(2)). Revocation: Parliament or the Council can revoke the delegation at any time. Delegated acts already in force stay valid (Article 97(3)). Consultation: before adopting a delegated act, the Commission must consult experts designated by each Member State, in line with the Interinstitutional Agreement of 13 April 2016 on Better Law-Making (Article 97(4)). Notification: the Commission must notify the act to Parliament and the Council at the same time (Article 97(5)). Entry into force: the act takes effect only if neither institution objects within three months of notification, or if both say earlier that they will not object. Either institution can extend that period by three months (Article 97(6)). Once an amendment is in force, the added or modified use-cases count as high-risk under Article 6(2), subject to the Article 6(3) derogation.

rows.question: Should market surveilance authorities be provided with remote access to documentations and data sets used to develop a high-risk AI system?
rows.answer: Yes. Article 74(12) requires providers to give market surveillance authorities full access to the documentation and to the training, validation and testing data sets used to develop a high-risk AI system. That access includes, "where appropriate and subject to security safeguards", application programming interfaces (API) or "other relevant technical means and tools enabling remote access". The right has limits set out in the same paragraph. Relevance and necessity: access applies "where relevant and limited to what is necessary to fulfil their tasks". Remote access is conditional: it is used where appropriate and only with security safeguards. Existing powers remain: the paragraph applies "without prejudice to" the authorities' powers under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020. Article 74(5) also lets authorities use the powers in Article 14(4), points (d) and (j), of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 remotely, as appropriate. Access to the source code is a separate and narrower right under Article 74(13). Authorities get it only on a reasoned request, and only when both of these conditions are met. Point (a): access is necessary to assess whether the system conforms with the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2. Point (b): testing, auditing and checks based on the provider's data and documentation have been exhausted or proved insufficient. Under Article 74(14), authorities must treat any information or documentation they obtain under the confidentiality obligations in Article 78.

rows.question: If a provider of a high-risk AI system confirms that the system achieves an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity at the time of development, then no further action is required by the provider on these aspects in the future. Correct?
rows.answer: No, that is not correct. Checking accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity once during development does not end the provider's duty. Under the AI Act, these are lifecycle obligations that continue after the system is placed on the market or put into service. Consistent performance over time: Article 15(1) requires high-risk AI systems to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. They must also "perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle." A result confirmed only at development does not meet this. Declared levels must stay true: Article 15(3) requires the levels of accuracy and the accuracy metrics to be declared in the instructions for use. Article 13(3)(b)(ii) adds that the instructions must state. The tested and validated levels of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity that can be expected; any known and foreseeable circumstances that may affect those levels. These declarations must remain accurate while the system is in use. Errors and systems that keep learning: Article 15(4) requires resilience against errors, faults or inconsistencies within the system or its environment, which may include technical redundancy such as backup or fail-safe plans. Systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or put into service must be developed to eliminate or reduce, as far as possible, biased outputs feeding back into future operation, with appropriate mitigation measures. This duty exists precisely because performance can change after release. Evolving attacks: Article 15(5) requires resilience against unauthorised third parties trying to change the system's use, outputs or performance by exploiting vulnerabilities. Where appropriate, this includes measures to prevent, detect, respond to, resolve and control the following. Data poisoning; model poisoning; adversarial examples or model evasion; confidentiality attacks; model flaws. Ongoing risk management: Article 9(1) requires the risk management system to be "established, implemented, documented and maintained." Article 9(2) describes it as a continuous, iterative process run throughout the entire lifecycle, with regular systematic review and updating. Under Article 9(2)(c), this includes evaluating risks that emerge from post-market monitoring data. Quality management: Article 17(1)(d) requires examination, test and validation procedures "before, during and after" development, with a set frequency. Article 17(1)(h) requires a post-market monitoring system, and Article 17(1)(a) requires procedures for managing modifications to the system. Staying compliant and correcting problems: Article 16(1)(a) requires providers to ensure the system complies with the Section 2 requirements, which include Article 15. Article 16(1)(j) requires corrective action and information duties if the system stops conforming. Changes after the first assessment: Article 13(3)(c) requires the instructions for use to describe any changes to the system and its performance that the provider pre-determined at the initial conformity assessment. Under Article 43(4), any other substantial modification triggers a new conformity assessment. A cybersecurity certificate or statement of conformity under Regulation (EU) 2019/881 creates a presumption of conformity with Article 15's cybersecurity requirements only as far as it covers them (Article 42(2)). It does not remove the provider's continuing lifecycle obligations.

rows.question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems avoid Chapter III high-risk requirements but retain Article 4 AI literacy duties, with voluntary codes under Article 95, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.

rows.question: Does "systemic risk" apply to AI systems or general purpose AI models or both?
rows.answer: Systemic risk applies to general-purpose AI models, not to AI systems. Under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as a model with systemic risk where it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; under Article 51(2) a model is presumed to have high impact capabilities where the cumulative computation used for its training exceeds 10^25 floating point operations. The Commission may also designate a model on the basis of the Annex XIII criteria. A model classified as having systemic risk then carries the additional Article 55 obligations: model evaluation including adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, serious-incident reporting, and adequate cybersecurity. The high-risk regime for AI systems under Articles 6 and Annex III is a separate classification and does not use the systemic-risk concept.

rows.question: Are AI systems that fall under one of the areas of Annex III, but not falling within a use-case within such areas, considered high-risk?
rows.answer: No. An AI system that only operates within one of the areas of Annex III, without matching one of the use-cases listed there, is not high-risk under Article 6(2). Article 6(2) makes high-risk only the "AI systems referred to in Annex III". Annex III does not list whole areas. Each numbered heading is followed by specific use-cases, and only those listed use-cases trigger the classification. Most areas have lettered points: biometrics (1(a), (c)), education (3(a), (d)), employment (4(a), (b)), essential services (5(a), (d)), law enforcement (6(a), (e)), migration (7(a), (d)) and justice and democratic processes (8(a), (b)). Critical infrastructure (Annex III(2)) has no lettered points, so its one described use applies directly: AI systems used as safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity. Two examples show the limits. An AI tool used in an educational institution for a purpose not listed in Annex III(3)(a), (d) is not high-risk under Article 6(2). The same is true of an employment-related tool that does not recruit or select people and does not do anything listed in Annex III(4)(b): making decisions on work terms, promotion or termination, allocating tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits, or monitoring and evaluating workers' performance and behaviour. Some use-cases also carry their own limits, so a system can be in the area and still fall outside the listed use. Biometrics, law enforcement and migration: these areas apply only "in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law" (Annex III(1), (6) and (7)). Biometric verification: systems whose sole purpose is to confirm that a person is who they claim to be are excluded (Annex III(1)(a)). Financial fraud detection: excluded from the creditworthiness use-case (Annex III(5)(b)). Travel document verification: excluded from the migration identification use-case (Annex III(7)(d)). Campaign administration tools: tools whose output people are not directly exposed to, such as tools used to organise political campaigns, are excluded (Annex III(8)(b)). The Article 6(3) derogation matters only for systems that do match a listed use-case. Such a system is still not high-risk if it poses no significant risk of harm and meets one of four conditions. (a) it performs a narrow procedural task; (b) it improves the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) it detects decision-making patterns or deviations from them, without replacing or influencing the earlier human assessment without proper human review; or. (d) it performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to the Annex III use-cases. A system that profiles natural persons is always high-risk. A provider relying on the derogation must document its assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service, and is subject to registration under Article 49(2) (Article 6(4)). A system outside the Annex III use-cases can still be high-risk under Article 6(1). That applies if it is a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the EU product-safety laws listed in Annex I (Union harmonisation legislation), and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment.

rows.question: Can an operator that is not a provider according to the EU AI Act, for example a deployer, take actions on a given high-risk AI system such that it can be effectively seen as a provider by the authorities? If yes, what kind of action would result in such an outcome?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).

rows.question: If I have an AI system that is high-risk because listed in the use cases of Annex III, and change it to a different use case that is not in Annex I or III, does it stay high-risk due to its historical provenance?
rows.answer: No, the system does not stay high-risk because of its history. Classification under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 depends on the system's current intended purpose, not on its earlier use. Why the earlier classification does not carry over. Annex III route (Article 6(2)): Only "AI systems referred to in Annex III" are high-risk. Every Annex III entry is written as AI systems "intended to be used" for a specific purpose. If the new intended purpose is not one of the use cases listed under the eight areas of Annex III, Article 6(2) no longer applies. Nothing in Article 6 keeps a system high-risk because it used to fall under Annex III. Annex I route (Article 6(1)): The system would be high-risk again only if both conditions are met. It is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I, or is itself such a product; and. That product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. If the new use does not meet both conditions, this route does not apply either. Article 6(3) and 6(4): You don't need the derogation in Article 6(3), or the documented assessment in Article 6(4). Both only apply to systems that are still "referred to in Annex III". Conditions for this to hold. The change must be real and documented. The new purpose has to show in what you, as provider, actually define and communicate: the instructions for use, promotional material and technical documentation. If the system is still offered, configured or documented for its former use, it still falls under that Annex III use case. Adding a new use while the old one stays available does not remove the classification. The new purpose must not fall under another Annex III entry. Many entries are broad. Examples include "to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of persons" in work-related relationships (point 4(b)) and risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance (point 5(c)). If the new use still matches any entry, the system stays high-risk. The only way out is then the Article 6(3) derogation, which is never available if the system profiles natural persons. Past compliance does not disappear. Units already placed on the market or put into service for the Annex III purpose were high-risk at that time. The obligations that attached to those units, such as post-market monitoring and incident reporting (Articles 72 to 73), still apply to them. The reclassification only affects the system as placed on the market or put into service for its new purpose.

If the new use case falls outside both Annex I and Annex III, neither condition in Article 6(1) or 6(2) is met, so the system is not high-risk

rows.question: How are AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum classified, and what exception is given for certain campaign-related tools?
rows.answer: Under Annex III point 8(b), AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum, or the voting behaviour of natural persons in exercising their vote, are high-risk under Article 6(2). Annex III point 8(b) itself excludes systems to whose output natural persons are not directly exposed, such as tools used only to organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view, which therefore fall outside this high-risk category.

rows.question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Under Article 1(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Act's objective is to improve how the internal market works and to promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence. It must do this while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and the fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection. That protection is against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union, and the Act must also support innovation. To achieve this, Article 1(2) states that the Regulation lays down. (a) harmonised rules for placing AI systems on the market, putting them into service and using them in the Union; (b) prohibitions of certain AI practices; (c) specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems; (d) harmonised transparency rules for certain AI systems; (e) harmonised rules for placing general-purpose AI models on the market; (f) rules on market monitoring, market surveillance, governance and enforcement; (g) measures to support innovation, with a particular focus on SMEs, including start-ups.

Promote uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI
Ensure high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights (incl. democracy, rule of law, environment) against harmful effects of AI systems
Support innovation

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which specific AI systems are explicitly listed as high-risk because they make decisions in critical life- and health-related situations involving emergency calls and triage?
rows.answer: Under Annex III point 5(d), AI systems intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls by natural persons, or to be used to dispatch or to establish priority in the dispatching of emergency first response services (including by police, firefighters and medical aid), as well as emergency healthcare patient triage systems, are explicitly listed as high-risk. They fall within the 'essential private and public services' category of the eight Annex III high-risk areas and are classified as high-risk through the Annex III route of Article 6(2), which treats any system falling within a listed use case as high-risk. That classification triggers the Chapter III Section 2 obligations for high-risk systems.

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, as part of their supervisory role for an AI regulatory sandbox, compliance with which specific Article must the market surveillance authority verify?
rows.answer: The market surveillance authority must verify compliance with Article 60, which covers testing high‑risk AI systems in real world conditions. This applies where that testing is done for AI systems supervised within an AI regulatory sandbox under Article 58. Article 76(2) says the authorities "shall verify the compliance with Article 60 as part of their supervisory role for the AI regulatory sandbox". This follows from Article 76(1), which gives them the powers to make sure such testing complies with the Regulation. Article 76(2) also allows a limited exception. The authorities may, as appropriate, let the provider or prospective provider run the testing without meeting two of the conditions in Article 60(4). Point (f): the time limit on how long the testing may last. Point (g): the requirement that test subjects from groups vulnerable because of their age or disability are appropriately protected. All other Article 60 conditions still apply and must still be verified. These include those in Article 60(4)(a) and (b): a real‑world testing plan must be drawn up and submitted to the authority, and the authority must approve it.

rows.question: Is an AI system used to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
rows.answer: No. Structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task, so the system falls under the Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a) derogation and is not high-risk, provided it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and does not materially influence the outcome of decision making; the other limbs are (b) improving the result of a previously completed human activity, (c) detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, and (d) performing a preparatory task, and the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons. Under Article 6(4) a provider relying on the derogation must document the assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and register it under Article 49(2).

However, under Article 6(3) such a system is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons.

rows.question: Regarding the European Artificial Intelligence Board: (1) Who designates its members? (2) How long is the term? How many times is the term renewable? (3) must members represent stakeholder interests or act impartially/objectively? (4) what voting threshold is required to adopt the Board's rules of procedure (is a simple 50%+1 majority enough)?
rows.answer: The European Artificial Intelligence Board (Article 65) has one representative per Member State, each serving a three-year term renewable once under Article 65(3). Under Article 65(4) each is their Member State's single contact point rather than an independent stakeholder appointee, while Article 65(7) requires the Board to safeguard the objectivity and impartiality of its activities. Its rules of procedure are adopted by a two-thirds majority under Article 65(5), so a simple majority is not sufficient.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?
rows.answer: The Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine on a provider of a general-purpose AI model, and it may cancel, reduce or increase the fine (Article 101(5)). This covers any decision fixing a fine under Article 101(1). Under that paragraph, the Commission can fine a provider up to 3% of its total worldwide annual turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher. The fine requires a finding that the provider, intentionally or negligently, did one of the following. Infringed the relevant provisions of the Regulation (point (a)); failed to comply with a request for a document or information under Article 91, or supplied incorrect, incomplete or misleading information (point (b)); failed to comply with a measure requested under Article 93 (point (c)); failed to give the Commission access to the model for an evaluation under Article 92 (point (d)). Unlimited jurisdiction means the Court is not limited to confirming or annulling the decision. It can look at the amount again itself. When setting the amount, the Commission must consider the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement, the principles of proportionality and appropriateness, and any commitments made under Article 93(3) or in codes of practice under Article 56 (Article 101(1)). Fines must also be effective, proportionate and dissuasive (Article 101(3)). Before adopting a fining decision, the Commission must send its preliminary findings to the provider and give it an opportunity to be heard (Article 101(2)). The Commission will also adopt implementing acts setting out detailed arrangements and procedural safeguards for these proceedings (Article 101(6)).

Court may cancel the fine
Court may reduce the fine
Court may increase the fine

rows.question: Consider the situation in which a market surveillance authority (MSA) determines that an AI system, originally classified as non-high-risk by the provider, is in fact high-risk. Does the provider need to recall and suspend the use of the system without undue delay, or does the MSA provide a timeframe within which the provider can take corrective actions? Or does this depend on the gravity of the situation?
rows.answer: No, the Act does not require the provider to recall or suspend the system automatically. Under Article 80(2), once the MSA finds that a system the provider classified as non-high-risk is in fact high-risk, the MSA must, without undue delay, require the provider to do two things. The provider must take all necessary actions to bring the system into compliance with the Regulation. It must also take appropriate corrective action within a period the MSA may prescribe. So the MSA sets the timeframe and decides what corrective action fits the case. Neither is fixed in the Act. Duties during that period. Compliance: Under Article 80(4), the provider must make sure the system is brought into compliance. If that does not happen within the Article 80(2) period, the provider is subject to fines under Article 99. All affected systems: Under Article 80(5), the corrective action must cover every system concerned that the provider has made available on the Union market. Other Member States: Under Article 80(3), if the system's use is not limited to the MSA's own country, the MSA must promptly tell the Commission and the other Member States what it found and what it has required of the provider. Suspension or recall only comes later, if the provider fails to act. Under Article 80(6), Article 79(5) to (9) applies where the provider does not take adequate corrective action in time. The MSA must then take all appropriate provisional measures. These can prohibit or restrict the system being made available or put into service on its national market, or withdraw or recall it. The MSA must notify the Commission and the other Member States. If nobody objects within three months, the measure is treated as justified. If there is an objection, the Commission decides under Article 81. Gravity does matter, in three ways. The MSA's discretion: Article 80(2) lets the MSA choose both the "appropriate" corrective action and the length of the period. It can therefore demand faster or stronger action, including withdrawal or recall, when the harm is greater. Risky systems follow a stricter procedure: If the system also presents a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights under Article 79(1), the Article 79(2) procedure applies. That procedure expressly covers withdrawal and recall, with a deadline set by the MSA. The deadline is in any event capped at the shorter of 15 working days or the period in the relevant Union harmonisation legislation. The provider's own duty is immediate: Under Article 20(1), a provider that has reason to consider its high-risk system non-conforming must immediately take the necessary corrective action. That means bringing the system into conformity, withdrawing it, disabling it or recalling it, "as appropriate". The provider must also inform distributors and, where applicable, deployers, the authorised representative and importers. Under Article 20(2), where the system presents a risk, the provider must also immediately investigate the causes and inform the competent MSA. It must also inform the notified body that certified the system, where applicable. The MSA's finding will normally give the provider that reason, so waiting for the deadline is not a safe position. Deliberate misclassification brings extra fines. Under Article 80(7), if the MSA establishes that the provider misclassified the system to avoid the high-risk requirements in Chapter III, Section 2, the provider faces fines under Article 99. These apply on top of the corrective action.

Failure to comply within that period triggers fines under Article 99 (and Article 79(5)-(9) applies), not gravity-based variation of the timeframe

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what presumption applies when a high-risk AI system is trained and tested on data that reflects the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting in which it is intended to be used?
rows.answer: Adds two further presumptions of conformity beyond Articles 40-41: Article 42(1), high-risk AI systems trained and tested on data reflecting the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual, or functional setting in which they are intended to be used are presumed to comply with the relevant data-governance requirements of Article 10(4); Article 42(2), high-risk AI systems certified or for which a statement of conformity has been issued under a cybersecurity scheme under Regulation (EU) 2019/881 (the Cybersecurity Act) and whose references are published in the Official Journal are presumed to comply with the cybersecurity requirements of Article 15 to the extent the cybersecurity certificate or statement covers those requirements. rows.answer: ‘AI regulatory sandbox’ means a controlled framework set up by a competent authority which offers providers or prospective providers of AI systems the possibility to develop, train, validate and test, where appropriate in real-world conditions, an innovative AI system, pursuant to a sandbox plan for a limited time under regulatory supervision;

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what transparency obligation applies to deployers when they use an AI system to generate or manipulate text for the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest, and what are the two exceptions where this obligation does not apply?
rows.answer: Under Article 50(4), a deployer that uses an AI system to generate or manipulate text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated. rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, when a high-risk AI system is found to conform with the requirements, what information must the Union technical documentation assessment certificate contain?
rows.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Under the EU AI Act, must an employer inform affected workers and workers' representatives before putting into service or using a high-risk AI system in the workplace?
If so, should possibly specific rules or procedures be followed to provide this information?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 26(7), a deployer that is an employer must, before putting a high-risk AI system into service or using it at the workplace, inform the workers' representatives and the affected workers that they will be subject to the use of that high-risk AI system. Under Article 26(7), that information must be provided, where applicable, in accordance with the rules and procedures laid down in Union and national law and practice on the information of workers and their representatives.

Recipients: workers' representatives and affected workers
Procedure: follow applicable Union/national law and practice on informing workers, where applicable (no separate free-standing procedure)

rows.question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
rows.answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. These conditions apply in addition to, and not instead of, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680. Article 10(5) requires all of the following: the bias work cannot be done with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data (a); technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation (b); strict controls and documentation of access so that only authorised persons under appropriate confidentiality obligations can reach the data (c); the data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties (d); deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first (e); and records of processing documenting why it was strictly necessary (f).

Strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations, with no transmission/transfer/access by other parties
Deletion once bias corrected or retention period ends, whichever is first
Processing records document necessity and why other data would not suffice
Additional to, not a substitute for, obligations under GDPR, EUDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what specific information must a provider/prospective provider submit (and keep up to date) regarding testing of a high-risk AI system in real-world conditions outside an AI regulatory sandbox?
rows.answer: Before testing an Annex III high-risk AI system in real world conditions outside a sandbox, the provider or prospective provider must submit a real-world testing plan to the market surveillance authority and register the testing with a set of identifying information. It must then keep that information current and report any extension, serious incidents, suspension or termination, and the final outcomes. Real-world testing plan (Article 60(4)(a)). The provider or prospective provider must draw up a real-world testing plan. It must submit the plan to the market surveillance authority in the Member State where the testing will take place. Testing may start only once that authority has approved both the testing and the plan (Article 60(4)(b)). If the authority does not answer within 30 days, both count as approved. This does not apply where national law has no tacit approval, in which case authorisation is still needed. The Commission will set out the detailed contents of the plan in implementing acts (Article 60(1)). Registration (Article 60(4)(c)). The testing must be registered in the EU database under Article 71(4), with a Union-wide unique single identification number. The information required by Annex IX, which must be provided and then kept up to date, is. The Union-wide unique single identification number of the testing; the name and contact details of the provider or prospective provider, and of the deployers involved; a brief description of the AI system, its intended purpose, and other information needed to identify it; a summary of the main characteristics of the testing plan; information on any suspension or termination of the testing. Exceptions to the registration rule (Article 60(4)(c)). Two groups of systems are registered differently. Law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control (Annex III points 1, 6 and 7): registration goes in the secure non-public section of the EU database. It includes only the information listed in Article 49(4), point (d), which covers Annex IX points 1, 2, 3 and 5. The summary of the testing plan is left out. Critical infrastructure (Annex III point 2): registration follows Article 49(5), which means at national level. Ongoing information duties. Extension: testing may last no longer than needed and at most six months. One further six-month extension is allowed, but only with prior notification to the market surveillance authority explaining why it is needed (Article 60(4)(f)). Serious incidents: these must be reported to the national market surveillance authority under Article 73 (Article 60(7)). Suspension, termination and results: the provider must notify the market surveillance authority of any suspension or termination of the testing and of the final outcomes (Article 60(8)). Requests: the provider must supply information when the market surveillance authority asks for it, using the powers conferred under Article 75 (Article 60(6)). Article 57 does not add any submission duties here. It covers testing inside a sandbox, which runs under a sandbox plan agreed with the competent authority (Article 57(5)).

Registration of the testing with a Union-wide unique single identification number
General rule: registration under Article 71(4) with information specified in Annex IX

Exceptions: Annex III points 1, 6, 7 (law enforcement/migration/asylum/border control) register in secure non-public EU database section per Article 49(4)(d); Annex III point 2 systems register per Article 49(5)

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, if a deployer has reason to believe that the use of a high-risk AI system may present a risk, what must the deployer do, and whom must the deployer inform?
rows.answer: Under Article 26(5) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the deployer must do two things without undue delay. Inform both of these. The provider or the distributor, and. The relevant market surveillance authority. Suspend its use of the high-risk AI system. When the duty applies. It applies where the deployer has reason to consider that using the system in accordance with the instructions for use may cause it to present a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1). That means a risk to the health, safety or fundamental rights of persons. How the deployer spots the risk. The duty sits within the deployer's general obligation under Article 26(5), first subparagraph, to monitor the system's operation on the basis of the instructions for use. There is one carve-out. A deployer that is a financial institution subject to internal-governance requirements under Union financial services law is deemed to meet that monitoring obligation by following those governance rules. What happens next on the provider side. Once the provider becomes aware of the risk, Article 20(2) requires it to immediately investigate the causes, working with the reporting deployer where applicable. The provider must also inform the competent market surveillance authorities and, where applicable, the notified body that issued the certificate.

Inform the relevant market surveillance authority
Suspend use of the system
All actions taken without undue delay

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider of a high-risk AI system supply to the deployer in the instructions for use? List the required categories of information.
rows.answer: Under Article 13(3), a provider of a high-risk AI system must supply instructions for use that contain at least the information listed below. Under Article 13(2), the instructions must come in a suitable digital format or another form. They must be concise, complete, correct and clear, and relevant, accessible and understandable to deployers. The required content is. (a) Provider identity: the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, of its authorised representative. (b) Characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, including. (i) the intended purpose; (ii) the level of accuracy, including its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity under Article 15, against which the system has been tested and validated and which can be expected, plus any known and foreseeable circumstances that may affect that level; (iii) any known or foreseeable circumstance that may lead to risks to health and safety or fundamental rights under Article 9(2), whether in use for the intended purpose or under reasonably foreseeable misuse; (iv) where applicable, the technical capabilities and characteristics that provide information relevant to explaining the system's output; (v) when appropriate, its performance for the specific persons or groups of persons it is intended to be used on; (vi) when appropriate, specifications for the input data, or other relevant information about the training, validation and testing data sets used, taking into account the intended purpose; (vii) where applicable, information that lets deployers interpret the output and use it appropriately. (c) Pre-determined changes: any changes to the system and its performance that the provider pre-determined at the initial conformity assessment. (d) Human oversight measures under Article 14, including the technical measures that help deployers interpret the system's outputs. (e) Resources, lifetime and maintenance: the computational and hardware resources needed, the expected lifetime, and any maintenance and care measures needed for proper functioning, with their frequency. This includes software updates. (f) Logging mechanisms: where relevant, a description of the mechanisms in the system that let deployers properly collect, store and interpret the logs under Article 12. Other provisions confirm some of these points. Article 15(3) requires the accuracy levels and relevant accuracy metrics to be declared in the instructions for use. Article 9(5)(c) treats providing the Article 13 information, and training deployers where appropriate, as a risk-management measure. When deciding what to include, the provider must consider the deployer's expected technical knowledge, experience, education and training, and the likely context of use.

Computational/hardware resources needed, expected lifetime, and maintenance/care measures
Description of logging mechanisms under Article 12, where relevant
