rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what actions must a provider take when it considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity with the Regulation?
rows.answer: A provider that considers, or has reason to consider, that a high-risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service does not conform with the Regulation must immediately take corrective action and inform the operators in its supply chain. If the system also presents a risk, the provider must investigate and notify the authorities. Article 16(1)(j) makes this a provider obligation ("take the necessary corrective actions and provide information as required in Article 20"). Article 20 sets out what it involves. Under Article 20(1), the provider must. Act immediately: take the necessary corrective actions, as appropriate, to bring the system into conformity, withdraw it, disable it, or recall it. Inform the supply chain: tell the distributors of the system. Where applicable, it must also inform the deployers, the authorised representative and the importers. Article 20(2) adds further steps where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) and the provider becomes aware of that risk. The provider must. Investigate: immediately investigate the causes, working with the reporting deployer where applicable. Notify authorities: inform the market surveillance authorities competent for that system. Where applicable, it must also inform the notified body that issued a certificate for the system under Article 44. The notice must cover, in particular, the nature of the non-compliance and any relevant corrective action taken.

Inform distributors of the system concerned
Where applicable, inform deployers, authorised representative and importers accordingly

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, what is the definition of (a) a "conformity assessment body" and (b) "conformity assessment"?
rows.answer: (a) Under Article 3(21) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, a "conformity assessment body" is "a body that performs third-party conformity assessment activities, including testing, certification and inspection." What makes it a conformity assessment body is that it acts as an independent third party, not as the provider. Under Article 3(22), a conformity assessment body becomes a "notified body" once it has been notified under the Regulation and other relevant Union harmonisation legislation. (b) Under Article 3(20), "conformity assessment" is "the process of demonstrating whether the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2 relating to a high-risk AI system have been fulfilled." The definition covers only high-risk AI systems and the requirements in Chapter III, Section 2. Article 43 sets out how the process works. It is either internal control by the provider under Annex VI, with no notified body, or an assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation with a notified body under Annex VII.

Conformity assessment body: activities include testing, certification and inspection
Conformity assessment: the process of demonstrating whether the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements for a high-risk AI system have been fulfilled
criterion_remarks: The answer states that a conformity assessment body performs third-party conformity assessment activities, which matches the substance of criterion 1.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 95, who may draw up codes of conduct, and which bodies must encourage and facilitate their drawing up?
rows.answer: Under Article 95(3), codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or by both. Any interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society organisations and academia, may be involved. A code may cover one or more AI systems, taking into account how similar their intended purposes are. Under Article 95(1), the AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct. This includes related governance mechanisms. The aim is to foster the voluntary application of some or all of the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements to AI systems other than high-risk AI systems, taking into account the available technical solutions and industry best practices. The Regulation as adopted gives this role to the AI Office, not to the Commission as a separate body. Under Article 95(2), the same bodies must also facilitate codes of conduct on the voluntary application of specific requirements to all AI systems, including by deployers. These codes must be based on clear objectives and key performance indicators that measure whether the objectives are met. Their elements include, without being limited to. Applicable elements of the Union ethical guidelines for trustworthy AI; assessing and minimising the impact of AI systems on environmental sustainability; promoting AI literacy; facilitating inclusive and diverse design of AI systems; assessing and preventing negative impacts on vulnerable persons or groups, including accessibility for persons with a disability and gender equality. Under Article 95(4), the AI Office and the Member States must take into account the specific interests and needs of SMEs, including start-ups, when they encourage and facilitate codes of conduct.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which AI systems in the financial services area are classified as high-risk under Annex III(5)(b), and what explicit exceptions are listed?
rows.answer: Under Annex III, point 5(b), the high-risk AI systems are those intended to be used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score. Article 6(2) makes any system listed in Annex III high-risk. The one explicit exception. Point 5(b) lists a single carve-out: AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud. A system used only for fraud detection does not fall under point 5(b), even when a credit or lending institution runs it. What the entry covers. It applies only to assessments of natural persons. Creditworthiness or credit-scoring of legal persons is not listed. Risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance is a separate entry under point 5(c), not part of point 5(b). Article 6(3) is a general rule, not an extra exception. It lets an Annex III system escape high-risk status if it poses no significant risk of harm and meets one of four conditions. It performs a narrow procedural task; it improves the result of a human activity that was already completed; it detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment; or. It performs a preparatory task. However, a system that profiles natural persons is always high-risk under the last subparagraph of Article 6(3). Credit scoring normally involves profiling, so this route will rarely apply to it. A provider who relies on Article 6(3) must document its assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service. That provider is also subject to registration under Article 49(2), and must hand over the documentation if national competent authorities ask for it (Article 6(4)).
criteria_text: AI systems evaluating creditworthiness or establishing credit score of natural persons
Exception: AI systems used for detecting financial fraud
criterion_remarks: The answer states that AI systems intended to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score are classified as high-risk under Annex III(5)(b).
The answer explicitly identifies the exception for AI systems used for detecting financial fraud, noting that such systems do not fall under Annex III(5)(b).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider established outside the EU do in order to place a high-risk AI system on the Union market?
rows.answer: A provider established outside the EU must first appoint an authorised representative established in the Union, by written mandate, before making its high-risk AI system available on the Union market (Article 22(1)). It must also meet all the same substantive and procedural requirements as a provider based in the EU. The authorised representative (Article 22). The provider must enable the representative to perform the tasks in the mandate (Article 22(2)). The representative must perform those tasks and give market surveillance authorities a copy of the mandate on request, in an official EU language indicated by the competent authority (Article 22(3)). The mandate must empower the representative to. (a) check that the EU declaration of conformity and the technical documentation have been drawn up, and that the provider has carried out an appropriate conformity assessment; (b) keep the following available to competent authorities for 10 years after placing on the market or putting into service: the provider's contact details, a copy of the declaration of conformity, the technical documentation and, where applicable, the notified body certificate; (c) on a reasoned request, give a competent authority all information and documentation needed to show conformity with the Section 2 requirements. This includes access to the automatically generated logs, to the extent the provider controls them; (d) on a reasoned request, cooperate with competent authorities in any action on the system, in particular to reduce and mitigate its risks; (e) where applicable, handle registration under Article 49(1), or, if the provider registers itself, make sure the information in point 3 of Section A of Annex VIII is correct. The mandate must also allow competent authorities to deal with the representative, in addition to or instead of the provider, on all compliance issues (Article 22(3)). The representative must end the mandate if it considers, or has reason to consider, that the provider is breaching its obligations. It must then immediately tell the relevant market surveillance authority and, where applicable, the notified body, giving its reasons (Article 22(4)). The system's design and development. Risk management: a documented, iterative risk management system covering the whole lifecycle. Testing against predefined metrics and probabilistic thresholds must happen before placing on the market (Article 9(1), (2) and (8)). Data governance: training, validation and testing data sets must meet the data governance and quality criteria (Article 10). Technical documentation: drawn up before placing on the market, kept up to date, and containing at least the Annex IV elements (Article 11(1)). Logging: the system must technically allow automatic recording of events (logs) over its lifetime (Article 12(1), (2)). Transparency and instructions: the system must be transparent enough for deployers and come with instructions for use (Article 13). Human oversight: effective human oversight must be possible (Article 14). Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity: appropriate levels must be achieved (Article 15). Quality management: the provider must run a quality management system (Article 17). Before placing the system on the market. Conformity assessment: carry out the applicable procedure under Article 43, either internal control or a notified body procedure, depending on the system (Article 43). Declaration of conformity: draw up a written, machine-readable, signed and dated EU declaration of conformity containing the Annex V information (Article 47). CE marking: affix it visibly, legibly and indelibly, followed by the notified body's identification number where applicable (Article 48). Registration: register the provider and the system in the EU database. The authorised representative may do this where applicable (Article 49). After placing the system on the market. Post-market monitoring: set up and document a monitoring system and plan (Article 72). Serious incidents: report them to the market surveillance authorities of the Member State where the incident happened (Article 73). The deadlines are. Immediately, and within 2 days of becoming aware, for a widespread infringement or serious disruption of critical infrastructure; within 10 days for a death; within 15 days for other serious incidents. In practice, distributors will not make the system available until they have checked that it bears the CE marking and comes with the declaration of conformity and instructions for use (Article 24(1)).

Representative empowered per Article 22(3) tasks (verify conformity documentation, retain records 10 years, provide information/log access to authorities, cooperate with authorities, handle registration)

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.
rows.answer: Under Article 17(1), providers of high-risk AI systems must have a quality management system (QMS) that ensures compliance with the Regulation. It must be documented in a systematic and orderly manner, as written policies, procedures and instructions. At a minimum, it must include all of the following. (a) a strategy for regulatory compliance, including compliance with conformity assessment procedures and procedures for managing modifications to the high-risk AI system; (b) techniques, procedures and systematic actions for design, design control and design verification; (c) techniques, procedures and systematic actions for development, quality control and quality assurance; (d) examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after development, and how often they must be carried out; (e) technical specifications, including standards, to be applied; where the relevant harmonised standards are not applied in full or do not cover all the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, the means used to ensure the system meets those requirements; (f) systems and procedures for data management, covering data acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation, retention and any other data operation performed before, and for the purpose of, placing on the market or putting into service; (g) the risk management system referred to in Article 9; (h) the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system in accordance with Article 72; (i) procedures for reporting a serious incident in accordance with Article 73; (j) handling communication with national competent authorities, other relevant authorities (including those providing or supporting access to data), notified bodies, other operators, customers and other interested parties; (k) systems and procedures for keeping records of all relevant documentation and information; (l) resource management, including security-of-supply measures; (m) an accountability framework setting out the responsibilities of management and other staff for all of the aspects above. Article 17 adds three qualifiers. Proportionality (Article 17(2)): How these aspects are implemented must be proportionate to the size of the provider's organisation. Providers must still meet the degree of rigour and level of protection needed for their high-risk AI systems to comply with the Regulation. Sectoral QMS (Article 17(3)): Providers that already have QMS obligations, or an equivalent function, under relevant sectoral Union law may include these aspects in that existing QMS. Financial institutions (Article 17(4)): Financial institutions subject to internal-governance requirements under Union financial services law are deemed to meet the QMS obligation by complying with those governance rules. This does not cover points (g), (h) and (i), which they must still meet in full. Any harmonised standards referred to in Article 40 must be taken into account. Frameworks such as ISO 9001 and ISO/IEC 42001 can help structure a QMS. However, they do not replace the statutory elements listed in Article 17(1).

Design, development, quality control and verification techniques/procedures
Examination, test and validation procedures and their frequency
Data management procedures across data lifecycle
Article 9 risk management system and Article 72 post-market monitoring system
Record-keeping and accountability framework for management/staff

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what additional obligations apply to providers of a general-purpose AI model that is classified as a model with systemic risk?
rows.answer: Providers of a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk must meet four extra obligations under Article 55(1). These apply "in addition to the obligations listed in Articles 53 and 54". A model has systemic risk under Article 51(1) if it has high-impact capabilities (point (a)) or the Commission designates it so based on the Annex XIII criteria (point (b)). Under Article 51(2), high-impact capabilities are presumed where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations. The four obligations are. Model evaluation (Article 55(1)(a)): evaluate the model using standardised protocols and tools that reflect the state of the art. This includes carrying out and documenting adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks. Systemic risk assessment and mitigation (Article 55(1)(b)): assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level, including their sources. This covers risks arising from the model's development, placing on the market or use. Serious incident reporting (Article 55(1)(c)): track, document and report serious incidents and possible corrective measures. Reports go without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national competent authorities. Cybersecurity (Article 55(1)(d)): ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for both the model and its physical infrastructure. The baseline duties in Article 53(1) still apply in full. Technical documentation under Annex XI (point (a)); information and documentation for downstream AI system providers, containing at least the Annex XII elements (point (b)); a policy to comply with Union copyright law, including respecting reservations of rights under Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 (point (c)); a sufficiently detailed public summary of training content, using the AI Office template (point (d)). Article 53(2) normally exempts models released under a free and open-source licence from points (a) and (b). That exemption expressly does not apply to models with systemic risk, so open-source status does not remove those duties. Under Article 55(2), providers can show compliance with the Article 55(1) duties by relying on codes of practice under Article 56, until a harmonised standard is published. Complying with European harmonised standards gives a presumption of conformity to the extent the standards cover those duties. Providers that neither follow an approved code nor comply with a harmonised standard must show other adequate means of compliance for the Commission to assess. Under Article 55(3), any information or documentation obtained under Article 55, including trade secrets, is subject to the confidentiality obligations in Article 78.

Assess and mitigate possible Union-level systemic risks, including their sources
Track, document and report serious incidents and corrective measures to the AI Office/national competent authorities without undue delay
Ensure adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what are the four grounds on which non-compliance with the Act may be alleged (as listed in Article 79(6))?
rows.answer: Article 79(6) sets out four grounds. When a market surveillance authority notifies the Commission and the other Member States of provisional measures under Article 79(5), it must say whether the non-compliance is due to one or more of the following. Prohibited AI practices: non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices in Article 5 (Article 79(6)(a)). High-risk requirements: a failure of a high-risk AI system to meet the requirements in Chapter III, Section 2 (Article 79(6)(b)). Flawed standards: shortcomings in the harmonised standards or common specifications in Articles 40 and 41 that confer a presumption of conformity (Article 79(6)(c)). Transparency obligations: non-compliance with Article 50 (Article 79(6)(d)). The notification must also give all available details. This includes the information needed to identify the non-compliant AI system, its origin and supply chain, the nature of the alleged non-compliance and the risk involved. It also covers the nature and duration of the national measures taken and the arguments put forward by the relevant operator (Article 79(6)).
criteria_text: Non-compliance with prohibition of AI practices under Article 5
Failure of high-risk AI system to meet Chapter III, Section 2 requirements
Shortcomings in harmonised standards/common specifications under Articles 40-41
Non-compliance with Article 50
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states non-compliance with the prohibition of AI practices under Article 5.
The answer clearly identifies failure of a high-risk AI system to meet requirements in Chapter III, Section 2.
The answer refers to shortcomings in harmonised standards or common specifications under Articles 40 and 41 conferring presumption of conformity.
The answer explicitly states non-compliance with Article 50 as one of the grounds.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement is banned by Article 5(1)(h). The only exception is where the use is strictly necessary for one of three objectives, and this list is exhaustive. Victims and missing persons: a targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation of human beings, and the search for missing persons (Article 5(1)(h)(i)). Threats to life or terrorism: preventing a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, or a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack (Article 5(1)(h)(ii)). Criminal suspects: locating or identifying a person suspected of a criminal offence, for a criminal investigation, a prosecution or the execution of a criminal penalty (Article 5(1)(h)(iii)). Two conditions apply. The offence must be listed in Annex II. The list covers terrorism; trafficking in human beings; sexual exploitation of children and child pornography; illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances; illicit trafficking in weapons, munitions or explosives; murder and grievous bodily injury; illicit trade in human organs or tissue; illicit trafficking in nuclear or radioactive materials; kidnapping, illegal restraint or hostage-taking; crimes within the International Criminal Court's jurisdiction; unlawful seizure of aircraft or ships; rape; environmental crime; organised or armed robbery; sabotage; and participation in a criminal organisation involved in any of these offences. The offence must be punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order with a maximum of at least four years. Even for these objectives, every use must meet cumulative conditions. National law: the use is only possible if a Member State chooses to allow it in its national law, and that law may be stricter than the Act (Article 5(5)). Purpose: the system may be used only to confirm the identity of the specifically targeted individual (Article 5(2)). Assessment: the authority must weigh how serious, likely and large the harm would be if the system were not used, against the consequences for the rights and freedoms of everyone affected (Article 5(2)(a), (b)). Safeguards: the use must follow the necessary and proportionate safeguards set by national law, especially limits on time, place and the persons covered (Article 5(2)). Before use: the law enforcement authority must complete a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and register the system in the EU database under Article 49. In duly justified urgent cases, registration can follow without undue delay (Article 5(2)). Authorisation: each use needs prior authorisation from a judicial authority, or an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding (Article 5(3)). In duly justified urgent cases, use may start without it, but authorisation must be requested within 24 hours. If authorisation is refused, use must stop immediately, and all data, results and outputs must be discarded and deleted. No decision with an adverse legal effect on a person may be based solely on the system's output. Notification: each use must be notified to the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority (Article 5(4)).
criteria_text: Targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, or missing persons
Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat
Localisation/identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or executing a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least 4 years custodial sentence/detention order
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the permitted objective of a targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, or missing persons, matching the substance of criterion 1.

The answer clearly identifies the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, or a genuine terrorist threat, as a permitted objective, satisfying criterion 2.

The answer specifies that locating or identifying a suspect is allowed only for an offence listed in Annex II and punishable by at least four years’ custodial sentence or detention order, covering the full substance of criterion 3.

rows.question: Under Article 32 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, when is a conformity assessment body presumed to comply with the requirements in Article 31?
rows.answer: Under Article 32, a conformity assessment body is presumed to comply with the requirements in Article 31 when it shows that it meets the criteria in the relevant harmonised standards, or parts of them, whose references have been published in the Official Journal of the European Union. The presumption has two limits. Only for published standards: it depends on the body showing it meets the relevant harmonised standards whose references are published in the Official Journal. Only as far as the standards go: it applies "in so far as the applicable harmonised standards cover those requirements". For any Article 31 requirement a standard does not cover, the body gets no presumption and must show compliance directly. The Article 31 requirements it can cover are. Being established under national law with legal personality (Article 31(1)); organisational, quality management, resource, process and cybersecurity requirements (Article 31(2)); a structure and operation that ensure confidence in its performance (Article 31(3)); independence from the provider, other operators with an economic interest and the provider's competitors (Article 31(4)); not being involved in the design, development, marketing or use of high-risk AI systems, including consultancy (Article 31(5)); safeguards for impartiality (Article 31(6)); confidentiality and professional secrecy (Article 31(7)); procedures proportionate to the provider's size, sector and structure and the AI system's complexity (Article 31(8)); liability insurance, unless the Member State assumes liability or is directly responsible for the assessment (Article 31(9)); professional integrity and competence (Article 31(10)); enough internal competence and permanently available personnel (Article 31(11)); taking part in coordination activities and keeping up to date on standardisation (Article 31(12)).
criteria_text: Body demonstrates conformity with relevant harmonised standards (or parts thereof)
Condition: references to those standards published in the Official Journal of the European Union
Presumption limited to the extent those standards cover the Article 31 requirements
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the body must demonstrate conformity with relevant harmonised standards or parts thereof.
The answer specifies that the presumption applies only when the references to those standards are published in the Official Journal of the European Union.
The answer explicitly limits the presumption to the extent that the applicable harmonised standards cover the Article 31 requirements, noting that for uncovered requirements, no presumption applies.

rows.question: Who is entitled to lodge a complaint about an infringement, and to which authority must the complaint be submitted?
rows.answer: Who can complain: Under Article 85, any natural or legal person may lodge a complaint if they have grounds to consider that there has been an infringement of the provisions of this Regulation. The complainant does not have to show that the infringement affected them personally. The only threshold is having grounds to believe that some provision of the AI Act has been infringed. Where the complaint goes: Complaints must be submitted to the relevant market surveillance authority. How complaints are handled: Under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020, the authority must take complaints into account when carrying out its market surveillance activities. It must also handle them under the dedicated procedures that market surveillance authorities have set up for complaints. Other remedies: This right applies without prejudice to other administrative or judicial remedies. A complaint under Article 85 adds to those routes and does not replace them.

Grounds to consider there has been an infringement of the Regulation
Submitted to the relevant market surveillance authority

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Under Article 50(2) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, providers of AI systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content, including general-purpose AI systems, must ensure that the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and are detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. Quality criteria. Article 50(2) also requires the technical solution to be. Effective. Interoperable. Reliable. These criteria apply as far as this is technically feasible. The provision lists the factors that shape that standard. The specific features and limits of different types of content. The costs of implementation. The generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards. Exceptions. Article 50(2) sets three carve-outs. The duty does not apply to the extent that the AI system. Performs an assistive function for standard editing; does not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or its meaning (the Act says "semantics"); or. Is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. Relationship to other rules. Under Article 50(6), this duty does not affect the Chapter III requirements and obligations. It is also without prejudice to other transparency obligations in Union or national law. Implementation. Under Article 50(7), the AI Office must encourage and facilitate codes of practice at Union level on detecting and labelling artificially generated or manipulated content. The Commission may approve those codes by implementing act under the procedure in Article 56(6). If it considers a code inadequate, it may instead adopt an implementing act setting common rules for these obligations under the examination procedure in Article 98(2).

Marking must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated
Solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable, as far as technically feasible
Feasibility judged against content-type specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and state of the art
Exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input data/semantics, or law-enforcement authorisation
criterion_remarks: The answer states that outputs must be marked in a machine-readable format.
The answer explicitly says outputs must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.
The answer lists effectiveness, interoperability, reliability, and robustness as required qualities, noting they apply as far as technically feasible.

The answer clearly outlines the three exemptions: assistive editing functions, no substantial alteration of input or semantics, and law enforcement authorisation.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what is the scientific panel of independent experts, what are its main support/advisory tasks, and what key characteristics/selection requirements apply to its members?
rows.answer: The scientific panel is a body of independent experts that supports enforcement of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. The Commission must set it up by an implementing act adopted under the examination procedure in Article 98(2) (Article 68(1)). That implementing act must also set the conditions, procedures and detailed arrangements for the panel and its members to issue alerts and to ask the AI Office for help with the panel's tasks (Article 68(5)). The panel advises and supports the AI Office, in particular with the following tasks (Article 68(3)). (a) General-purpose AI: supporting implementation and enforcement of the Regulation for general-purpose AI models and systems, in particular by. (i) alerting the AI Office to possible systemic risks at Union level from general-purpose AI models, in accordance with Article 90; (ii) contributing to tools and methodologies for evaluating the capabilities of general-purpose AI models and systems, including through benchmarks; (iii) advising on the classification of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk; (iv) advising on the classification of various general-purpose AI models and systems; (v) contributing to the development of tools and templates. (b) Market surveillance: supporting the work of market surveillance authorities, at their request. (c) Cross-border activities: supporting cross-border market surveillance under Article 74(11), without prejudice to the powers of market surveillance authorities. (d) Union safeguard procedure: supporting the AI Office's duties in the Union safeguard procedure under Article 81. The Commission selects the experts based on up-to-date scientific or technical expertise in AI needed for these tasks. Each expert must be able to show all of the following (Article 68(2)). (a) particular expertise and competence, and scientific or technical expertise, in the field of AI; (b) independence from any provider of AI systems or general-purpose AI models; (c) an ability to carry out activities diligently, accurately and objectively. The Commission, in consultation with the Board, decides how many experts the panel needs and must ensure fair gender and geographical representation (Article 68(2)). Once appointed, the experts must meet these conduct requirements (Article 68(4)). They must act with impartiality and objectivity. They must keep information and data obtained in their work confidential. They must neither seek nor take instructions from anyone when carrying out their Article 68(3) tasks. Each expert must draw up a declaration of interests, which is made public. The AI Office must set up systems and procedures to actively manage and prevent conflicts of interest. The panel is separate from the Article 67 advisory forum. The forum is made up of stakeholders chosen to give a balanced mix of interests, while the panel's experts must be independent of providers.

Tasks: advise/support AI Office on general-purpose AI models (alerting systemic risks under Article 90, developing evaluation tools/benchmarks, advising on classification); plus support market surveillance authorities, cross-border surveillance (Article 74(11)), and Union safeguard procedure (Article 81)
Selection: experts chosen by Commission for up-to-date scientific/technical AI expertise, independence from any AI provider, and ability to act diligently, accurately and objectively
Members must act impartially, confidentially and free of instructions, each publishing a declaration of interests

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, if a provider identifies a serious incident during testing in real-world conditions of a high-risk AI system, what three actions must the provider take?
rows.answer: Under Article 60(7) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the provider or prospective provider must take three actions. Report the incident. The serious incident must be reported to the national market surveillance authority in accordance with Article 73. That means reporting immediately once a causal link, or a reasonable likelihood of one, is established. The general limit is 15 days after becoming aware of the incident (Article 73(2)). If a person has died, the limit is 10 days (Article 73(4)). For a widespread infringement or a serious incident under Article 3, point (49)(b), the limit is two days (Article 73(3)). An incomplete first report may be sent, followed by a complete report (Article 73(5)). Mitigate, suspend or terminate. The provider must adopt immediate mitigation measures. Failing that, it must suspend the testing in real world conditions until mitigation takes place, or otherwise terminate the testing. Set up a recall procedure. The provider must establish a procedure for the prompt recall of the AI system if the testing is terminated. If the testing is suspended or terminated, Article 60(8) also requires the provider to notify the national market surveillance authority of the suspension or termination and of the final outcomes.
criteria_text: Report the serious incident to the national market surveillance authority in accordance with Article 73
Adopt immediate mitigation measures or, failing that, suspend the testing until mitigation takes place, or otherwise terminate it
Establish a procedure for the prompt recall of the AI system upon termination of the testing
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that the serious incident must be reported to the national market surveillance authority in accordance with Article 73, including timing details from that provision.
The answer clearly states the requirement to adopt immediate mitigation measures, and if that fails, to suspend or terminate testing—matching the substance of the criterion.
The answer explicitly states that the provider must establish a procedure for the prompt recall of the AI system upon termination of testing.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which body has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Chapter V), and which entity is entrusted with implementing those tasks?
rows.answer: Under Article 88(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the European Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V, which sets out the obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models. When it uses these powers, it must take into account the procedural guarantees in Article 94. The AI Office is the entity the Commission must entrust with implementing these tasks (Article 88(1)). This does not affect the Commission's own powers of organisation, or how competences are divided between the Member States and the Union under the Treaties. National market surveillance authorities do not enforce Chapter V directly. Under Article 88(2), and without prejudice to Article 75(3), they may ask the Commission to use its Chapter V enforcement powers. They can do so where that is necessary and proportionate to help them carry out their own tasks under the Regulation.

AI Office is entrusted with implementing these tasks
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer explicitly states that the European Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V.

rows.question: What must a distributor do if it considers a high-risk AI system is not in conformity with the Act's requirements? Additionally, what extra steps are required if the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1)?
rows.answer: What a distributor must do depends on whether it has already made the system available. In both cases the duty applies where the distributor "considers or has reason to consider, on the basis of the information in its possession," that a high-risk AI system does not meet the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2. Before making the system available (Article 24(2)): The distributor must not make the system available on the market until it has been brought into conformity with those requirements. After making the system available (Article 24(4)): The distributor must take one of three corrective actions: bring the system into conformity, withdraw it, or recall it. It may instead ensure that the provider, the importer or any relevant operator takes those actions. Extra steps where the system presents a risk under Article 79(1): Such a system is a "product presenting a risk" under Article 3, point 19, of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020, to the extent it poses risks to people's health, safety or fundamental rights. Before the system is made available (Article 24(2)): The distributor must also inform the provider or the importer, as applicable, of that risk. After the system is made available (Article 24(4)): The distributor must immediately inform the provider or importer and the authorities competent for that system. It must give details, in particular of the non-compliance and of any corrective actions taken.
criteria_text: Not make it available on market until brought into conformity
If risk under Art 79(1): immediately inform provider or importer and the competent authorities
Notification must detail the non-compliance and any corrective actions taken
criterion_remarks: The answer discusses actions before and after making the system available, but does not state that the distributor must not make it available until conformity is achieved in the post-availability context; instead, it describes corrective actions like withdrawal or recall, which do not equate to the requirement in criterion 1.

The answer clearly states that if the system presents a risk under Article 79(1), the distributor must immediately inform the provider or importer and the competent authorities after the system is made available, which matches the substance of the criterion.
The answer explicitly mentions that the notification must include details, in particular of the non-compliance and of any corrective actions taken, satisfying the requirement in the criterion.

rows.question: Under Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), which categories of actors/persons does the Act apply to? List the categories.
rows.answer: Under Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Act applies to seven categories of actors and persons. Providers (Article 2(1)(a)): providers placing on the market or putting into service AI systems, or placing on the market general-purpose AI models, in the Union. This applies whether those providers are established or located within the Union or in a third country. EU deployers (Article 2(1)(b)): deployers of AI systems that have their place of establishment or are located within the Union. Third-country providers and deployers (Article 2(1)(c)): providers and deployers of AI systems established or located in a third country, where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union. Importers and distributors (Article 2(1)(d)): importers and distributors of AI systems. Product manufacturers (Article 2(1)(e)): product manufacturers placing on the market or putting into service an AI system together with their product and under their own name or trademark. Authorised representatives (Article 2(1)(f)): authorised representatives of providers that are not established in the Union. Affected persons (Article 2(1)(g)): affected persons that are located in the Union. The rest of Article 2 narrows this personal scope. Under Article 2(10), the Regulation does not apply to obligations of deployers who are natural persons using AI systems in a purely personal non-professional activity. Under Article 2(4), it does not apply to public authorities in a third country or to international organisations that would otherwise fall under paragraph 1. This exclusion covers only their use of AI systems under international cooperation or agreements for law enforcement and judicial cooperation with the Union or Member States. It also requires that the third country or organisation provides adequate safeguards for fundamental rights and freedoms.

Deployers of AI systems established/located in the Union
Providers and deployers in third countries where the AI system's output is used in the Union
Importers, distributors, and product manufacturers (placing an AI system on the market/into service with their product under their own name/trademark)
Authorised representatives of providers not established in the Union
Affected persons located in the Union
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that providers placing on the market or putting into service AI systems or placing on the market GPAI models in the Union are covered, including those located inside or outside the Union.

The answer includes providers and deployers in third countries where the AI system's output is used in the Union, matching the criterion's substance.
The answer separately lists importers, distributors, and product manufacturers placing AI systems on the market or into service under their own name or trademark, covering all three sub-elements.
The answer explicitly refers to authorised representatives of providers not established in the Union as a covered category.
The answer includes affected persons located in the Union as a category to which the Act applies.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what conditions must be met before data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions can be transferred to a third country (outside the EU)?
rows.answer: Data collected and processed for testing a high-risk AI system in real-world conditions may be sent to a third country only if appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are in place. This rule is in Article 60(4), point (e). It is one of the conditions in Article 60(4) that must all be met before a provider or prospective provider of a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III may run testing in real-world conditions outside an AI regulatory sandbox. The AI Act does not create its own transfer mechanism, and it does not list which safeguards count. Instead, it points to the safeguards that other Union law already requires. For personal data, that mainly means the GDPR's rules on transfers to third countries. Where the testing data includes special categories of personal data, the conditions of GDPR Article 9 also apply. If the transfer lacks the safeguards Union law requires, a condition of Article 60(4) is not met, and the testing itself is not permitted under Article 60. The transfer condition applies alongside the other conditions in Article 60(4). The provider or prospective provider must. Be established in the Union, or have appointed a legal representative established in the Union (point (d)); have drawn up a real-world testing plan and submitted it to the market surveillance authority where the testing will take place (point (a)); have that authority's approval, including tacit approval after 30 days where national law allows it (point (b)); have registered the testing as required (point (c)). Test subjects must also have given informed consent, except in the narrow law enforcement case set out in point (i). Separately, under Article 60(5), subjects can withdraw at any time and ask for their personal data to be deleted immediately and permanently.
criteria_text: Appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law must be implemented for the transfer
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer explicitly states that appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law must be implemented for the transfer, which matches the substance of the criterion.

rows.question: What are the three maximum administrative fine tiers for (a) prohibited AI practices, (b) non-compliance with obligations for high-risk AI systems and general-purpose AI (GPAI) models, and (c) supplying incorrect/incomplete/misleading information? For each tier, give the maximum amount in EUR and the alternative maximum as a percentage of worldwide annual turnover.
rows.answer: The three maximum fines are EUR 35 000 000 or 7 %, EUR 15 000 000 or 3 %, and EUR 7 500 000 or 1 %. Each percentage is of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, and the higher of the two amounts applies. (a) Prohibited AI practices: Under Article 99(3), breaching the Article 5 prohibitions can lead to a fine of up to EUR 35 000 000. If the offender is an undertaking, the cap is up to 7 % of its turnover, whichever is higher. (b) High-risk AI systems and GPAI models: The cap is up to EUR 15 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 3 % of turnover, whichever is higher. High-risk systems: Article 99(4) sets this cap for a closed list of obligations. It covers providers under Article 16, authorised representatives under Article 22, importers under Article 23, distributors under Article 24 and deployers under Article 26. It also covers notified bodies under Articles 31, 33(1), (3) and (4) and 34, and the transparency duties of providers and deployers under Article 50. GPAI model providers: The same tier applies, but the legal basis is different. Under Article 101(1), the Commission, not national authorities, may fine a provider up to 3 % of turnover or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher. This applies where the provider intentionally or negligently. Breached the relevant provisions of the Regulation; failed to comply with an Article 91 request for documents or information; failed to comply with a measure requested under Article 93; failed to give the Commission access to the model for an evaluation under Article 92. Start date: These Commission fines apply from 2 August 2026. (c) Incorrect, incomplete or misleading information: Under Article 99(5), supplying such information to notified bodies or national competent authorities in reply to a request can lead to a fine of up to EUR 7 500 000. For an undertaking, the cap is up to 1 % of turnover, whichever is higher. For GPAI providers, supplying such information to the Commission falls under Article 101(1)(b) instead, so the EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % cap applies. For SMEs, including start-ups, Article 99(6) reverses the rule: each Article 99 fine is capped at whichever of the fixed amount or the percentage is lower.
criteria_text: Prohibited AI practices (Article 5): up to EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever higher
High-risk/GPAI obligations (Articles 16, 22, 23, 24, 26, 31, 33(1)(3)(4), 34, 50): up to EUR 15,000,000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever higher
Incorrect/incomplete/misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities: up to EUR 7,500,000 or 1% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever higher

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what is the EU database for high-risk AI systems, what categories of information must it contain, and who is the controller of that database?
rows.answer: The EU database is a Union-wide register that the Commission sets up and maintains in collaboration with the Member States. It holds registrations of Annex III high-risk AI systems and of Annex III systems that providers have judged not to be high-risk. The Commission is the controller of the database (Article 71(6)). What the database covers. Article 71(1) sets its scope as. High-risk AI systems under Article 6(2), registered under Articles 49 and 60; AI systems that are not high-risk under Article 6(3), registered under Articles 6(4) and 49. The Commission must consult relevant experts when setting the database's functional specifications, and the Board when updating them (Article 71(1)). Who enters data. Under Article 71(2) and (3). Providers, or their authorised representatives, enter the data in Sections A and B of Annex VIII. Deployers that are, or act on behalf of, public authorities, agencies or bodies enter the data in Section C of Annex VIII (Article 49(3)). Categories of information. Annex VIII, Section A (providers of high-risk systems, Article 49(1)). The provider's name, address and contact details; details of any person submitting on the provider's behalf; details of the authorised representative, where applicable; the trade name and any unambiguous reference to the system; a description of the intended purpose and the components and functions supported; a basic description of the data or inputs used and the operating logic; the system's status (on the market, no longer on the market, or recalled); the type, number and expiry date of any notified-body certificate, and the notified body's name or ID; a scanned copy of that certificate; the Member States where the system is placed on the market, put into service or made available; a copy of the EU declaration of conformity; electronic instructions for use (not required for law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control systems); an optional URL for more information. Annex VIII, Section B (providers of systems exempted under Article 6(3), Article 49(2)). The provider's details; details of any person submitting on the provider's behalf; details of the authorised representative; the trade name and reference; the intended purpose; which Article 6(3) condition or conditions are relied on; a short summary of the grounds for the exemption; the system's status; the Member States concerned. Annex VIII, Section C (public-authority deployers, Article 49(3)). The deployer's details; details of any person submitting on the deployer's behalf; the URL of the provider's database entry for the system; a summary of the Article 27 fundamental rights impact assessment findings; where applicable, a summary of the data protection impact assessment. Annex IX (real-world testing, Article 60(4)(c)). The Union-wide unique single identification number of the test; the names and contact details of the provider or prospective provider and of the deployers involved; a brief description of the AI system and its intended purpose; a summary of the main characteristics of the testing plan; information on any suspension or termination of the test. Personal data. The database may contain personal data only as far as necessary. This includes the names and contact details of the people responsible for registering the system who have legal authority to represent the provider or deployer (Article 71(5)). Public by default: Article 49 registrations must be publicly available in a user-friendly, machine-readable and navigable form (Article 71(4)). Real-world testing: Article 60 registrations are open only to market surveillance authorities and the Commission, unless the prospective provider agrees to publication (Article 71(4)). Law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control: systems under Annex III points 1, 6 and 7 go in a secure non-public section. That section holds only the Annex VIII and Annex IX data points listed in Article 49(4), and only the Commission and the Article 74(8) authorities can see it. Critical infrastructure: systems under Annex III point 2 are registered at national level under Article 49(5), not in this database. Controller's duties. As controller, the Commission must also give providers, prospective providers and deployers adequate technical and administrative support. The database must meet applicable accessibility requirements (Article 71(6)).

Categories: Annex VIII Sections A and B entered by provider/authorised representative; Section C entered by deployer that is/acts on behalf of a public authority, agency or body
Controller: the Commission

rows.question: What are the conditions to classify general-purpose AI (GPAI) model as "GPAI model with systemic risk"? Do all need to be met at the same time?
rows.answer: No, the conditions do not all have to be met at the same time. Under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk "if it meets any of the following conditions." The two conditions are alternatives, so either one is enough. The one thing that is always required is that the model is a general-purpose AI model within the meaning of Article 3(63). That means an AI model that "displays significant generality and is capable of competently performing a wide range of distinct tasks" and that can be integrated into a variety of downstream systems or applications. Once that is the case, either of these conditions leads to classification. High-impact capabilities (Article 51(1)(a)). The model "has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks.". Under Article 3(64), "high-impact capabilities" means capabilities that "match or exceed the capabilities recorded in the most advanced general-purpose AI models.". Article 51(2) presumes a model has such capabilities when the cumulative computation used for its training, measured in floating-point operations, is greater than 10^25. This compute threshold is only a presumption within condition (a). It is not a separate, cumulative requirement. A model can also meet condition (a) through its evaluated capabilities, indicators and benchmarks. Commission decision (Article 51(1)(b)). The Commission decides that the model "has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those set out in point (a) having regard to the criteria set out in Annex XIII.". The Commission can act on its own initiative ("ex officio") or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel. This route can capture a model that does not itself show high-impact capabilities under point (a), or does not reach the compute presumption. Under Article 51(3), the Commission must adopt delegated acts to amend these thresholds and to add benchmarks and indicators when necessary, for example because of algorithmic improvements or more efficient hardware. The current criteria can therefore change over time. Once a model is classified this way, its provider must meet the Article 55(1) obligations in addition to those in Articles 53 and 54. These are. Model evaluation, including adversarial testing. Assessing and mitigating systemic risks at Union level. Tracking, documenting and reporting serious incidents. Adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. The free and open-source exception in Article 53(2) also stops applying.
criteria_text: Condition (a): high impact capabilities per Article 51(1)(a), presumed when training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs
Condition (b): Commission decision (ex officio or following qualified alert from scientific panel) that capabilities/impact are equivalent, per Annex XIII criteria
No, not cumulative - either condition alone suffices
criterion_remarks: The answer states that high-impact capabilities are evaluated based on technical tools and methodologies, and explicitly mentions the 10^25 FLOPs presumption from Article 51(2), which is directly linked to condition (a).

The answer clearly explains that the Commission can decide ex officio or following a qualified alert that a model has capabilities or impact equivalent to those in point (a), referring to the Annex XIII criteria as the basis for that assessment.
The answer explicitly states that the conditions are alternatives and that 'either one is enough', correctly conveying that they are not cumulative.

rows.question: For a high-risk AI system, who is responsible for ensuring that input data is relevant and sufficiently representative for the system's intended purpose, and under what condition does that responsibility apply?
rows.answer: The deployer is responsible for this, but only to the extent that it exercises control over the input data. Article 26(4) says that, without prejudice to Article 26(1) and (2), "to the extent the deployer exercises control over the input data," the deployer "shall ensure that input data is relevant and sufficiently representative in view of the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system.". The condition therefore depends on control. If the deployer does not control the input data, for example because the provider fixes or supplies it, this duty does not apply to the deployer. Where it does apply, it sits alongside the deployer's other Article 26 duties. The deployer must still use the system according to its instructions for use (Article 26(1)) and assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (Article 26(2)). The duty is separate from the provider's own data obligations. Training, validation and testing data: Article 10 requires the provider to ensure these data sets meet quality criteria, including being relevant and sufficiently representative. Presumption of conformity: under Article 42(1), a system trained and tested on data reflecting the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting of its intended use is presumed to comply with Article 10(4). Input data specifications: under Article 13(3)(b)(vi), the provider must include in the instructions for use, when appropriate, specifications for the input data. Those specifications help the deployer judge whether its input data fits the system's intended purpose.
criteria_text: The deployer of the high-risk AI system
Only to the extent the deployer exercises control over the input data
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the deployer is responsible for ensuring input data is relevant and sufficiently representative, which matches the substance of criterion 1.

The answer explicitly states the responsibility applies only to the extent the deployer exercises control over the input data, and explains that if the deployer does not control the data, the duty does not apply, satisfying criterion 2.

rows.question: I am a distributor of an AI systems. Do I have obligation not to jeopardize its conformity? I was not told if the system is high-risk or not. What if am I am importer instead?
rows.answer: Yes. As a distributor, the operator must ensure that storage or transport conditions do not jeopardise the system's compliance, but only if the system is a high-risk AI system. If you were the importer, you would have the same duty under a parallel provision, plus wider verification duties. Distributor. Under Article 24(3), while a high-risk AI system is under the operator's responsibility, the operator must ensure that storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise its compliance with the Section 2 requirements. This duty belongs to a wider set of distributor obligations. Before making it available (Article 24(1)): verify that the system. Bears the required CE marking; comes with a copy of the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47) and instructions for use; shows that the provider and any importer have met their duties under Article 16, points (b) and (c), and Article 23(3). If you think it may not conform (Article 24(2)): if you consider, or have reason to consider, based on the information you hold, that it does not conform, do not make it available until it has been brought into conformity. If it presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), inform the provider or the importer, as applicable. If it is already on the market (Article 24(4)): take the corrective action needed to bring it into conformity, withdraw it or recall it, or make sure the provider, importer or another relevant operator does so. If it presents an Article 79(1) risk, immediately inform the provider or importer and the competent authorities, with details of the non-compliance and any corrective action taken. Authorities: on reasoned request, give the competent authority information and documentation about the operator's actions under paragraphs 1 to 4 (Article 24(5)), and cooperate with authorities to reduce or mitigate the risk (Article 24(6)). Not knowing whether it is high-risk. Every duty in Articles 23 and 24 applies only to high-risk AI systems. If the system is not high-risk, these provisions, including the storage and transport duty, do not apply to the operator. This question stays open until the classification is clear. The checks in Article 24(1) are the practical way to find out. A CE marking and an EU declaration of conformity show that the provider treats the system as high-risk. If you have reason to believe the system is high-risk but those items are missing, the operator must not make it available until the system conforms (Article 24(2)). It is sensible to ask the provider in writing to confirm the classification. Importer. Article 23(4) sets out the same duty: while the high-risk AI system is under the operator's responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, must not jeopardise its compliance with Section 2. An importer's other obligations are broader than a distributor's. Before placing it on the market (Article 23(1)): verify that. The provider has carried out the Article 43 conformity assessment; the provider has drawn up the technical documentation under Article 11 and Annex IV; the system bears the CE marking and comes with the Article 47 EU declaration of conformity and instructions for use; the provider has appointed an authorised representative under Article 22(1). If you have sufficient reason to think there is a problem (Article 23(2)): if the system does not conform, is falsified or comes with falsified documentation, do not place it on the market until it conforms. If it presents an Article 79(1) risk, inform the provider, the authorised representative and the market surveillance authorities. The operator's identity (Article 23(3)): put the operator's name, registered trade name or trade mark, and contact address on the system and on its packaging or accompanying documentation, where applicable. Records (Article 23(5)): keep copies of any notified body certificate, the instructions for use and the EU declaration of conformity for 10 years after the system is placed on the market or put into service. Authorities: on reasoned request, provide all information and documentation needed to show conformity, in a language they can easily understand, and make sure the technical documentation can be made available (Article 23(6)). Cooperate with them to reduce and mitigate risks (Article 23(7)). As with a distributor, all of these importer duties apply only if the system is high-risk.
criteria_text: Yes, obligation applies regardless of high-risk knowledge
Distributor: storage/transport must not jeopardise Section 2 compliance (Article 24(3))
Importer: same obligation applies (Article 23(4))
criterion_remarks: The answer states the obligation applies only if the system is high-risk, and explicitly says the duties do not apply if the system is not high-risk, contradicting the criterion that the obligation applies regardless of knowledge about high-risk status.
The answer cites Article 24(3) and correctly states the distributor's obligation regarding storage/transport conditions not jeopardising Section 2 compliance for high-risk systems.
The answer identifies that the same storage/transport obligation applies to importers under Article 23(4), satisfying the substance of the criterion.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: No, it is not automatically high-risk. Being a safety component of a product covered by Annex I is only one of two conditions in Article 6(1). A Class I device of this kind normally fails the second condition. Under Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk only if both of these apply. Point (a): it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the legislation listed in Annex I. The Medical Devices Regulation (EU) 2017/745 is listed in Annex I, point 11, so this condition is met. Point (b): that product "is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment" under that Annex I legislation before it is placed on the market or put into service. This is where the device fails. The Medical Devices Regulation lets manufacturers of Class I devices that are not sterile, have no measuring function and are not reusable surgical instruments declare conformity themselves. No notified body is involved. Because the device needs no third-party conformity assessment, point (b) is not met and Article 6(1) does not make the AI system high-risk. Placing the AI system on the market separately from the device does not change this. The wording "irrespective of whether placed on the market or put into service independently" only removes any requirement that the system be sold with the product. It does not remove the third-party assessment condition. Two points could still change the result. The device's class. Point (b) looks at the actual class of the product. If the AI makes the device a higher class under the Medical Devices Regulation, the device may need a notified body. The same applies if the AI system is itself a medical device software product in a higher class, as software informing diagnostic or therapeutic decisions usually is. In either case point (b) would be met and the system would be high-risk under Article 6(1). Annex III. Article 6(2) makes a system high-risk on its own terms if its intended purpose is a use case listed in Annex III. For health-related AI, the relevant entries are. Annex III, point 5(a): public authorities assessing whether people are eligible for essential public benefits and services, including healthcare services. Annex III, point 5(d): assessing and classifying emergency calls, dispatching emergency first response services, and emergency healthcare patient triage systems. If an Annex III use case applies, the Article 6(3) derogation can still apply. The system is not high-risk if it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing decisions, and it meets one of four conditions. It performs a narrow procedural task; it improves the result of a previously completed human activity; it detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the earlier human assessment without proper human review; or. It performs a preparatory task for an assessment relevant to an Annex III use case. The derogation never applies if the system profiles natural persons. A provider relying on it must document its assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service. It must also register under Article 49(2) and give that documentation to national competent authorities on request (Article 6(4)).
criteria_text: No
Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are cumulative conditions
MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) devices undergo manufacturer self-assessment, not third-party conformity assessment
Condition (b) fails, so Article 6(1) does not apply
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'No, it is not automatically high-risk,' which matches the required verdict.
The answer explains that both conditions in Article 6(1) must be fulfilled and that they are not standalone, satisfying the substance of the criterion.
The answer clearly states that Class I devices of this type undergo manufacturer self-assessment and do not require a notified body, capturing the factual basis of the criterion.
The answer concludes that because point (b) is not met, Article 6(1) does not apply, directly stating the logical consequence required by the criterion.

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), can the same AI system be subject both to the Act's "high-risk AI system" obligations and to the transparency obligations sometimes described informally as "limited risk"? Explain briefly.
rows.answer: Yes, the same AI system can be subject to both sets of obligations. The Act's categories are not mutually exclusive tiers. They add up. Article 50(6) says that paragraphs 1 to 4 "shall not affect the requirements and obligations set out in Chapter III". That means a high-risk AI system still carries all its Chapter III obligations and must also meet any Article 50 transparency duty that applies to it. Article 50 is also without prejudice to other transparency obligations for deployers under Union or national law. A system is caught by Article 50 because of what it does, not because of its risk classification. Systems that interact with people (Article 50(1)): providers must make sure people are told they are dealing with an AI system. This does not apply where that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person. It also does not apply to systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards, unless the public can use them to report a crime. Synthetic content (Article 50(2)): providers of systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text must mark the outputs in a machine-readable format so they can be detected as artificially generated or manipulated. This does not apply to the extent the system performs an assistive function for standard editing, or does not substantially alter the deployer's input data or its semantics. It also does not apply where use is authorised by law for criminal-offence purposes. Emotion recognition and biometric categorisation (Article 50(3)): deployers must inform the people exposed to the system and process personal data under Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680, as applicable. This does not apply where use is permitted by law to detect, prevent or investigate criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards and in accordance with Union law. Deep fakes and public-interest text (Article 50(4)). Deployers must disclose that deep fake content is artificially generated or manipulated. This does not apply to use authorised by law for criminal-offence purposes. For evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous works, the duty is limited to disclosing the content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper display or enjoyment of the work. Deployers must disclose AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. It also does not apply where the text has undergone human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for publishing it. Under Article 50(5), the information must be given clearly and distinguishably, at the latest at the first interaction or exposure, and must meet applicable accessibility requirements. For example, an emotion recognition system classified as high-risk must comply with the Chapter III regime. Its deployer must also inform exposed people under Article 50(3). Meeting one set of obligations does not satisfy the other.
criteria_text: Yes
Article 50(6): Article 50(1)-(4) transparency duties do not affect Chapter III high-risk obligations
Obligations are cumulative, not mutually exclusive

The answer quotes and explains Article 50(6), stating it preserves Chapter III obligations, thereby conveying the substance of the provision.
The answer clearly states that the obligations 'add up' and that 'meeting one set of obligations does not satisfy the other,' conveying cumulativeness.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a toy qualify as a high-risk AI system, and if so under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 6(1), an AI system intended to be used as a toy can be a high-risk AI system. This is the Annex I product route, because Directive 2009/48/EC on the safety of toys is listed in Annex I, point 2. Both of the following conditions must be met. Condition (a), Article 6(1)(a): the AI system is itself a product covered by the Toy Safety Directive, or it is intended to be used as a safety component of such a toy. Condition (b), Article 6(1)(b): under that Directive, the toy (or the toy whose safety component is the AI system) must undergo a third-party conformity assessment before it is placed on the market or put into service. The classification applies whether or not the AI system is placed on the market or put into service separately from the toy. The Toy Safety Directive itself decides whether third-party assessment is required. If the manufacturer can lawfully rely on its own internal assessment, condition (b) is not met, and the toy is not high-risk on this route. It could still be high-risk under Article 6(2) if it performs a use listed in Annex III. The derogation in Article 6(3) does not apply to this route. It is expressly a derogation "from paragraph 2" and covers only Annex III systems. Its tests (a narrow procedural task, improving a completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns, or a preparatory task) therefore cannot take an AI toy that meets Article 6(1) out of the high-risk category. Conformity assessment. Under Article 43(3), the provider of such a high-risk AI toy follows the conformity assessment procedure required by the Toy Safety Directive. In addition. Section 2 requirements: the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 of the AI Act apply and form part of that assessment. Annex VII points: points 4.3, 4.4 and 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also apply. Notified bodies: bodies notified under the Toy Safety Directive may check compliance with Section 2. This is only if their compliance with Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11) was assessed during their notification. Opting out of third-party assessment: where the Directive lets the manufacturer opt out by applying all relevant harmonised standards, the manufacturer may do so only if it has also applied harmonised standards, or common specifications under Article 41, covering all Section 2 requirements. Under Article 43(4), a substantial modification of the system triggers a new conformity assessment. For systems that keep learning after release, changes the provider set in advance at the first assessment and recorded in the technical documentation under Annex IV, point 2(f), are not substantial modifications.

Condition: AI system is a toy or safety component of a toy covered by Directive 2009/48/EC (Annex I harmonisation legislation)
Condition: that toy is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under the Directive
Both conditions cumulative (Article 6(1))
