rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI system meant to be used as a safety component in a lift can be a high-risk AI system under Article 6(1). This happens when both conditions in that paragraph are met. The two conditions (Article 6(1)). Directive 2014/33/EU covers lifts and safety components for lifts. It is listed in Annex I, point 4, so a lift is a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I. Condition (a), Article 6(1)(a): the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a lift, or it is itself a product covered by that Directive. Condition (b), Article 6(1)(b): under Directive 2014/33/EU, the lift, or the AI system itself as a product, must undergo a third-party conformity assessment before it is placed on the market or put into service. If both conditions are met, the AI system is high-risk. This is so whether it is placed on the market or put into service on its own or together with the lift. If the Lifts Directive does not require a third-party conformity assessment for the product in question, this route does not make the system high-risk. The Article 6(3) exemption does not apply. Article 6(3) lets some systems avoid high-risk status, for example those doing a narrow procedural task or preparatory work. That exemption covers only systems that are high-risk because they are listed in Annex III under Article 6(2). It cannot be used for a lift safety component that is high-risk under Article 6(1). The related duty in Article 6(4) to document a "not high-risk" assessment does not apply either. Conformity assessment (Article 43(3)). Directive 2014/33/EU is in Section A of Annex I, so the provider follows the conformity assessment procedure required by that Directive. Within that procedure. The Section 2 requirements of Chapter III of the AI Act apply and are part of the assessment. Points 4.3, 4.4 and 4.5 of Annex VII, and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6, also apply. Notified bodies designated under the Lifts Directive may check the AI system against the Section 2 requirements. This is allowed only if their compliance with Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11) was assessed when they were notified. The Lifts Directive may let a manufacturer skip the third-party assessment by applying all relevant harmonised standards. In that case, the manufacturer may use that option only if it has also applied harmonised standards, or where applicable the common specifications under Article 41, covering all the Section 2 requirements.

Condition: that product (or the AI system itself as a product) required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation
Both conditions cumulative

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), are AI systems intended for emotion recognition from biometric data always prohibited? If not, in which contexts are they prohibited, what exception applies, and how are they classified when not prohibited?
rows.answer: Emotion recognition is not categorically prohibited under the AI Act; the prohibition in Article 5 only applies in workplaces and educational institutions, with a narrow medical/safety exception. Elsewhere the system is high-risk under Annex III.1(c) and triggers Article 50(3) transparency duties toward exposed persons.

Exception: use intended for medical or safety reasons
When not prohibited, classified as high-risk under Annex III (emotion recognition/biometrics category)

rows.question: I generated audio with AI for my artistic work (sole purpose). Do I need to provide some marking of its artificial nature? I feel that would compromise the enjoyment of the work.
rows.answer: Usually not in a way that would spoil the work. You only have to disclose if the audio counts as a "deep fake". Even then, for an evidently artistic work the disclosure can be kept out of the way of the listening experience. The operator is not a "deployer" at all if you use the AI system for a purely personal, non-professional activity (Article 3(4)). In that case Article 50 puts no duty on you. If you publish or sell the work in a professional context, the operator is a deployer, and the rules below apply. Article 50 has applied since 2 August 2026. The labelling duty depends on whether the audio is a deep fake (Article 50(4), first subparagraph). A deep fake is AI-generated or manipulated content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear authentic or truthful (Article 3(60)). A cloned voice of a real singer or a fake recording of a real person would qualify. Original synthetic music or voices that imitate no one would not, and you would have no duty to label them under Article 50. The artistic carve-out (Article 50(4), third subparagraph). If the audio is a deep fake but forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or similar work, you only have to disclose that such content exists. The operator can do this "in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work." A note in the credits, liner notes, the track description or the platform metadata would normally be enough. You do not need an audible warning inside the track. Other exception. The disclosure duty also does not apply where the law authorises the use to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences (Article 50(4)). That is not relevant here. The separate rule for AI-generated text on matters of public interest does not cover audio. Form and timing (Article 50(5)). Any disclosure you owe must be clear and distinguishable. It must be given no later than the first time someone hears the content, and it must meet the applicable accessibility requirements. The machine-readable marking is not the operator's job (Article 50(2)). The provider of the AI tool must make sure its output is marked in a machine-readable format that can be detected as AI-generated. This marking is technical and inaudible, so it does not affect how people enjoy the work. The provider's duty does not apply where the tool only assists with standard editing or does not substantially alter the operator's input. It also does not apply to uses authorised by law for criminal-offence purposes. You would only take on this duty if you were the provider yourself, for example if you built and released the generator. The high-risk rules (Article 6, Annex III), such as CE marking and conformity assessment, do not apply to making art.
criteria_text: Yes, disclosure still required
No need for marking that hampers enjoyment
Must disclose existence of AI-generated content in appropriate/unobtrusive manner
criterion_remarks: The answer states that disclosure is required if the audio is a deep fake and the use is professional, which affirms the obligation under Article 50(4).

rows.question: For AI systems that fit within the use cases listed in Annex III but are considered non-high-risk by the provider, do they need to be registered in the EU database?
rows.answer: Yes. An Annex III system that the provider considers not high-risk must still be registered in the EU database. The registration duty. Article 6(4) says a provider who considers an Annex III system not high-risk "shall be subject to the registration obligation set out in Article 49(2)". Under Article 49(2), before the system is placed on the market or put into service, the provider (or its authorised representative, where applicable) must register itself and the system in the EU database under Article 71. Documenting the assessment. Also under Article 6(4), the provider must document its assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service. It must hand that documentation over when national competent authorities ask for it. When the derogation applies. Article 6(3) lets a provider treat an Annex III system as not high-risk only if the system poses no significant risk of harm to people's health, safety or fundamental rights. That includes not materially influencing the outcome of decisions. The system must also meet at least one of four conditions. It performs a narrow procedural task; it improves the result of a human activity already completed; it detects decision-making patterns, or departures from earlier patterns, without replacing or influencing the earlier human assessment without proper human review; or. It performs a preparatory task for an assessment relevant to the Annex III use cases. Profiling. An Annex III system that profiles natural persons is always high-risk. In that case the provider registers under Article 49(1) as a high-risk system, not under Article 49(2). What goes into the database. Article 71(1) says the database covers systems not considered high-risk under Article 6(3) and registered under Article 6(4) and Article 49. Under Article 71(2), the provider or authorised representative enters the Section B data of Annex VIII. Restricted registration for some areas. For systems in Annex III points 1, 6 and 7 (biometrics, law enforcement, and migration, asylum and border control), Article 49(4) applies. Registration goes into a secure non-public section of the database. It includes only Section B, points 1 to 5, 8 and 9, of Annex VIII. Only the Commission and the national authorities in Article 74(8) can see it. In all other cases, Article 71(4) makes the registered information publicly available. Critical infrastructure (Annex III point 2). The carve-out in Article 49(1) and the national-level registration in Article 49(5) apply only to high-risk systems. Article 49(2), as adopted, has no such exception for point 2. Deployers. Public-authority deployers do not have to register a system that is not high-risk. Their duty under Article 49(3) covers only high-risk Annex III systems.
criteria_text: Yes
Registration required under Article 49(2)
Registered in EU database referred to in Article 71

The answer cites Article 49(2) as the basis for registration and explains its application to non-high-risk Annex III systems.
The answer clearly states that registration is in the EU database referred to in Article 71, and references Article 71(1) and (2) to confirm the database's relevance.

rows.question: Do I need informed consent to test a high-risk AI system in real-world conditions outside a regulatory sandbox?
rows.answer: Yes. You need informed consent in almost every case. If the operator is a provider or prospective provider of a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, you may test it in real-world conditions outside an AI regulatory sandbox only if all the conditions in Article 60(4) are met. Under Article 60(4), point (i), one of those conditions is that the test subjects have given informed consent in accordance with Article 61. What valid consent requires. Under Article 61(1), the operator must obtain freely-given informed consent from each test subject before they take part. First the operator must give them concise, clear, relevant and understandable information on. (a) the nature and objectives of the testing, and any inconvenience that participation may cause; (b) the conditions of the testing, including how long the subject is expected to take part; (c) their rights and the guarantees around their participation, in particular their right to refuse to take part, or to withdraw at any time, without any detriment and without giving a reason; (d) how to request the reversal or disregarding of the AI system's predictions, recommendations or decisions; (e) the Union-wide unique single identification number of the testing under Article 60(4), point (c), and the contact details of the provider or its legal representative for further information. Under Article 61(2), the consent must be dated and documented, and a copy must be given to the subject or their legal representative. Under Article 60(5), subjects or their legally designated representatives may withdraw at any time by revoking their consent. They need give no reason, suffer no detriment, and may request immediate and permanent deletion of their personal data. Withdrawal does not affect activities already carried out. The one exception: law enforcement. Article 60(4), point (i), allows testing without consent only in law enforcement, and only where asking for consent would prevent the AI system from being tested. In that case, the testing and its outcome must not have any negative effect on the subjects, and their personal data must be deleted after the test. Consent alone is not enough. The Article 60(4) conditions are cumulative. They also include. Drawing up a real-world testing plan and submitting it to the market surveillance authority in the Member State where the testing will take place (point (a)); that authority's approval, which is deemed given after 30 days without an answer, unless national law does not provide for tacit approval (point (b)); registering the testing (point (c)). Testing under Article 60 is also without prejudice to any ethical review required by Union or national law (Article 60(3)). For high-risk AI systems related to products covered by Annex I legislation, Article 60(1) leaves Union or national law on real-world testing unaffected. The Article 61 consent regime applies specifically to testing under Article 60. Real-world testing inside a sandbox is instead supervised under the sandbox plan agreed with the competent authority (Article 57(5)).
criteria_text: Yes

Consent must be freely given and informed, obtained prior to participation, covering nature/objectives/inconveniences, conditions and duration, rights to refuse/withdraw without detriment or justification, reversal/disregard arrangements, and the unique ID plus provider contact details
Consent must be dated, documented, and a copy given to the subject or their legal representative
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' and confirms that informed consent is required for real-world testing outside a sandbox, aligning with the criterion's required verdict.

The answer details each element of informed consent as listed in Article 61(1), covering all required components: nature/objectives/inconveniences, conditions/duration, rights to refuse/withdraw without detriment or justification, reversal/disregard arrangements, and unique ID plus provider contact details.

The answer cites Article 61(2) and explicitly states that consent must be dated, documented, and a copy given to the subject or their legal representative, which matches the substance of the criterion.

rows.question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
rows.answer: Neither duty waits for the market surveillance authority. Once a provider becomes aware that its high-risk AI system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), Article 20(2) requires it to immediately investigate the causes. It must also inform the authorities. Article 20(1) separately requires it to immediately take corrective action where it considers, or has reason to consider, that the system is not in conformity. The provider investigates at once (Article 20(2)). The provider must immediately investigate the causes itself, working with the reporting deployer where applicable. It must inform the market surveillance authorities competent for the system. Where applicable, it must also inform the notified body that issued a certificate for the system under Article 44. That information must cover, in particular, the nature of the non-compliance and any relevant corrective action taken. The words "corrective action taken" show that investigating, correcting and reporting are expected to run side by side, not one after another. The provider corrects at once when non-conformity is suspected (Article 20(1)). If the provider considers, or has reason to consider, that the system is not in conformity with the Regulation, it must immediately take the necessary corrective actions. The options are to bring the system into conformity, withdraw it, disable it or recall it, as appropriate. It must inform the distributors and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative and importers. The trigger here is reason to suspect non-conformity, not the mere existence of a risk. In practice, a risk under Article 79(1) will often give that reason, either straight away or once the investigation starts. The authority's procedure runs alongside, not instead (Article 79). Under Article 79(2), the authority carries out its own evaluation only when it has sufficient reason to consider that the system presents a risk. The relevant operators must cooperate as necessary. If the authority finds non-compliance, it must, without undue delay, require the operator to take all appropriate corrective actions: bring the system into compliance, withdraw it, or recall it. This must happen within the period it prescribes, and in any event within the shorter of 15 working days or the period in the relevant Union harmonisation legislation. Under Article 79(4), the operator must ensure that all appropriate corrective action is taken for all affected AI systems it has made available on the Union market. Under Article 79(5), if the operator does not take adequate corrective action within that period, the authority takes provisional measures. These can prohibit or restrict making the system available, withdraw it or recall it. So the operator's example has it backwards. The authority's evaluation is a check on the provider's own duties, not a replacement for them. If the risk has turned into a serious incident (Article 73(6)). After reporting under Article 73(1), the provider must, without delay, carry out the necessary investigations, including a risk assessment of the incident and corrective action. It must cooperate with the competent authorities and, where relevant, the notified body. Before informing the competent authorities, it must not carry out any investigation that alters the AI system in a way that could affect a later evaluation of the incident's causes.
criteria_text: Both
Immediate corrective action required under Article 20(1) where system is non-compliant
Immediate investigation of causes is the provider's own duty under Article 20(2)
Investigation done in collaboration with reporting deployer where applicable, not deferred to market surveillance authority
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that both immediate investigation and corrective action are required, confirming both duties apply.
The answer cites Article 20(1) and explains that corrective action is required immediately when non-conformity is suspected, including steps like withdrawal or recall.
The answer clearly assigns the duty to investigate causes to the provider under Article 20(2), stating it must happen immediately and that the provider must act itself.

The answer specifies that the provider must investigate in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and emphasizes that this duty is not deferred to the market surveillance authority.

rows.question: What is Article 50(4) about?
rows.answer: **Article 50(4) sets transparency duties for deployers (the people or organisations using an AI system) in two cases: AI-generated or manipulated deep fakes, and AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. Deep fakes. A deployer of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(4), first subparagraph). There are two qualifications. Criminal-law exception. The duty does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute a criminal offence. Artistic works. Where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme, the duty is lighter. The deployer only has to disclose that such generated or manipulated content exists. The disclosure must be made in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work. Public-interest text. A deployer of an AI system that generates or manipulates text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(4), fourth subparagraph). This duty does not apply in two cases. The use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences; or. The AI-generated content has undergone human review or editorial control, and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for publishing it. The human-review exception covers only this text duty. It does not excuse the deep-fake disclosure. How the disclosure must be made.** Under Article 50(5), the information must be given to the people concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner, at the latest when they first interact with or are exposed to the content. It must also meet the applicable accessibility requirements. Article 50(4) is separate from the providers' duty in Article 50(2) to mark synthetic outputs in a machine-readable, detectable format. Under Article 50(6), it does not affect the Chapter III requirements or other transparency obligations under Union or national law.
criteria_text: Deployers of AI systems generating/manipulating image, audio or video constituting a deep fake must disclose the content is artificially generated or manipulated
Exception where use is authorised by law to detect/prevent/investigate/prosecute criminal offences
For evidently artistic/creative/satirical/fictional/analogous works, obligation limited to disclosing existence of such content without hampering enjoyment/display

Separate rule: deployers of AI systems generating/manipulating text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose artificial generation, with exceptions for law-enforcement authorisation or human review/editorial responsibility
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that deployers of AI systems generating or manipulating deep fake content must disclose the artificial generation or manipulation.
The answer clearly identifies the exception when use is authorised by law for criminal offence detection, prevention, investigation, or prosecution.
The answer correctly explains the limited disclosure obligation for artistic, creative, satirical, or fictional works and specifies that disclosure must not hamper enjoyment or display.

The answer accurately describes the separate rule for AI-generated text published for public interest, including both exceptions: law enforcement authorisation and human review with editorial responsibility.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear sections without self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Is an AI system high-risk if it is used in a product that: is not listed in Annex I; use case not listed in Annex III; internally uses general purpose AI model with systemic risk due to high impact capabilities?
rows.answer: No. The AI system is not high-risk. Using a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk inside it does not change that. Under Article 6, an AI system can be high-risk in only two ways. Annex I route (Article 6(1)): Both conditions must be met. Under point (a), the system is a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I. Under point (b), that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. The operator's product is not covered by Annex I, so this route fails. Annex III route (Article 6(2)): The system is used for one of the purposes listed in Annex III. the operator's use case is not listed, so this route also fails. The Article 6(3) exception, and the rule that profiling is always high-risk, only apply to systems already within Annex III, so neither is relevant here. Neither route looks at the model inside the system. Systemic-risk status is a label for the general-purpose AI model itself. It creates duties for the model's provider under the Act's separate rules for such models, not a high-risk label for the systems built on it. The operator's system therefore does not have to meet the high-risk requirements (risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, conformity assessment, post-market monitoring). The system is not free of the Act, though. It must not carry out any practice banned by Article 5(1)(a), (h). If it matches an Article 50 case, it also has transparency duties. People interacting with the system must be told it is AI. Synthetic audio, image, video or text must be marked in a machine-readable, detectable way. This does not apply where the system only assists with standard editing, does not substantially change the deployer's input or its meaning, or is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute crimes. Deployers of emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems must inform the people exposed to them. Deployers must disclose deepfakes and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. The system would only become high-risk if its intended purpose changed so that it met the Article 6(1) or Article 6(2) conditions.
criteria_text: No
Article 6(1) not met: not an Annex I product/safety component requiring third-party conformity assessment
Article 6(2) not met: use case not listed in Annex III
Internal use of a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk is not an Article 6 criterion
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No. The AI system is not high-risk,' which matches the required verdict.
The answer explains that the product is not covered by Annex I, so the conditions of Article 6(1) are not met, stating the substance of the criterion.
The answer explicitly states that the use case is not listed in Annex III, hence Article 6(2) does not apply, conveying the required substance.
The answer clarifies that internal use of a systemic-risk general-purpose AI model is not a criterion under Article 6 for high-risk classification, directly addressing the substance of the criterion.

rows.question: My local small language model says that, as a distributor of high-risk AI systems, I must be careful that transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance. But AI is just software, isn't it? So I am pretty sure my model hallucinated. What do you say?
rows.answer: No, the operator's model did not hallucinate. Article 24(3) says that distributors "shall ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise the compliance of the system with the requirements set out in Section 2.". The words "where applicable" answer the operator's point about software. The duty covers storage or transport conditions only when they could actually affect the system. A system distributed purely as a download may raise few or no such issues. But the Act does not treat high-risk AI systems as software only. Many are built into physical products, or ship on hardware, sensors, devices or storage media. Heat, moisture, shock, tampering or a damaged storage medium could harm those parts, or the integrity of the software on them. That damage could undermine the Section 2 requirements the system must meet. The duty applies only while the system is under the operator's responsibility, so it covers the operator's own handling and does not make you answer for the whole supply chain. The duty also connects to the rest of Article 24. Before you make the system available: if you consider, or have reason to consider, that it no longer conforms with Section 2 (for example, because of storage or transport damage), the operator must not make it available until it has been brought into conformity (Article 24(2)). If the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), the operator must also inform the provider or importer. After you have made it available: the operator must take the corrective actions needed to bring it into conformity, withdraw it or recall it, or ensure that the provider, importer or another relevant operator does so (Article 24(4)). Where there is an Article 79(1) risk, the operator must immediately inform the provider or importer and the competent authorities, giving details of the non-compliance and any corrective actions taken. Authority requests: on a reasoned request, the operator must give the competent authority the information and documentation about the operator's actions under Article 24(1) to (4) (Article 24(5)). Cooperation: the operator must cooperate with the competent authorities in any action they take on the system (Article 24(6)).
criteria_text: No, not hallucinated
Article 24(3) applies
Duty applies only 'where applicable' (e.g., embedded/supplied hardware or physical media)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that the model did not hallucinate, affirming the correctness of the local model's statement.
The answer cites and applies Article 24(3), explaining its relevance to the distributor's obligations regarding transport and storage conditions.

The answer explains that the duty applies only 'where applicable', clarifying that it depends on whether storage or transport conditions could affect compliance, particularly in cases involving hardware or physical media.

rows.question:
Given an AI system that is high-risk according to Annex III: if it is repurposed to a use case not in Annex III (nor Annex I), then:
- the repurposed AI system is still high-risk due to reversibility of training into the original system
- the repurposed AI system is no longer high-risk but it must be reported in the EU database
- the repurposed AI system is no longer high-risk and there is no need to report it in the EU database
rows.answer: The third option is correct: the repurposed AI system is no longer high-risk, and it does not need to be registered in the EU database. No lasting high-risk status. Under Article 6(2), a system is high-risk because it is one of the "AI systems referred to in Annex III", and every Annex III entry is defined by use ("AI systems intended to be used for "). Once the system's intended purpose no longer matches any Annex III use case, Article 6(2) stops applying. The Act has no rule that keeps high-risk status because the training could be reversed to rebuild the original system. So the first option has no legal basis. No Annex I route either. Article 6(1) makes a system high-risk only if both of these are true. It is a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I (point (a)); and. That product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment (point (b)). The question rules out Annex I, so this route is closed. No database registration. Article 71(1) sets out what the EU database holds, and there are only two categories. High-risk AI systems under Article 6(2), registered under Articles 49 and 60; and. Annex III systems the provider considers not high-risk under the Article 6(3) derogation, registered under Article 6(4) and Article 49. The repurposed system is in neither category. It is not an Annex III system at all, so it is not using the Article 6(3) derogation. That derogation only covers systems that stay within Annex III, and it never applies to a system that profiles natural persons. This is why the second option is wrong. The database duty for the original Annex III system still applies to that system while it remains on the market or in service for its Annex III purpose.
criteria_text: No longer high-risk (third option)
High-risk status attaches to intended purpose/use case under Article 6(2)/Annex III, not to the system or its training as such
New use case outside Annex III and Annex I means neither limb of Article 6 is satisfied
No registration/EU database obligation (Article 49/Article 71) since system is not high-risk
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the repurposed system is no longer high-risk and does not need to be reported, matching the third option.
The answer explains that high-risk status under Article 6(2) depends on the intended purpose as defined in Annex III, not on the system's training or technical history.
The answer confirms that neither Article 6(1) (Annex I) nor Article 6(2) (Annex III) applies to the new use case, so the system no longer meets any high-risk criterion.
The answer correctly states that database registration under Articles 49 and 71 only applies to high-risk systems or those using the Article 6(3) derogation, neither of which applies here.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose with logical flow, suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: We have a phone system where the caller can press 1 if they consent to the call being recorded, 2 if they do not. We wish to replace this with an NLP system that understands a voice reply like "Yes", "Sure", "Please no", etc. Would such a system be considered high-risk? It's for our clinic.
rows.answer: No, it would not be high-risk. A voice system that only works out whether a caller agrees to be recorded is not high-risk under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. The Act makes a system high-risk in only two ways, and this system meets neither. The product route (Article 6(1)). This applies only if both conditions in Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are met. The AI system is a safety component of a product covered by the laws listed in Annex I, or is itself such a product; and. That product must be checked by a third party under those laws. Among the laws in Annex I are the Medical Devices Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (Annex I.11) and the In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (Annex I.12). A tool that records consent on a phone line has no medical purpose and is not a safety component of a medical device. Being used in a clinic does not change that. The listed-uses route (Article 6(2) and Annex III). This applies only if the system matches one of the specific uses listed under the eight areas of Annex III. It matches none of them. The closest ones do not fit. Annex III.5(a) covers systems used by or for public authorities to decide whether people are eligible for essential public benefits and services, including healthcare. Capturing consent decides nothing about access to care. Annex III.5(d) covers systems that assess and classify emergency calls, set dispatch priority, or triage emergency patients. The operator's system does none of these. Annex III.1 covers biometrics: remote biometric identification, biometric categorisation and emotion recognition. Understanding what a caller says ("Yes", "Sure", "Please no") is none of these. Because the system is not listed in Annex III, you don't need the Article 6(3) exemption. Even if it were listed, it would likely qualify, because it does a narrow procedural task (Article 6(3)(a)) and does not profile anyone. When the answer would change. Keep the system's intended purpose narrow. It could become high-risk if it were extended to. Identify callers by their voice (Annex III.1(a)); infer callers' emotions from their voice (Annex III.1(c)); or. Triage or prioritise urgent medical calls (Annex III.5(d)). If you, as the deployer, changed the purpose of a system that is not high-risk so that it became high-risk, you would be treated as its provider under Article 25(1)(c). You would then take on all of the provider's obligations. What still applies outside the AI Act. Not being high-risk doesn't settle whether a spoken reply counts as valid consent. Whether "Sure" is freely given and unambiguous, and how you record, store and let people withdraw consent to recording, falls under data-protection law (the GDPR) and national rules on recording calls. A clinic handles health-related data, so you need a reliable fallback when a reply is unclear, such as asking again or offering the keypad option. You also need a record of what the system decided.
criteria_text: No
Not biometric categorisation or emotion recognition under Annex III(1)(b)-(c), since the system parses semantic content (yes/no), not emotional or protected-attribute inference
Not essential healthcare services under Annex III(5)(a), since consent capture for call recording is not an eligibility evaluation for benefits/services
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No, it would not be high-risk,' which unambiguously matches the required verdict.

The answer explains that understanding spoken 'Yes', 'Sure', or 'Please no' involves parsing semantic content, not inferring emotions or protected attributes, and explicitly states this is not biometric categorisation or emotion recognition under Annex III(1)(b)-(c).

rows.question: Does the EU AI Act establish a "proportionality of need" requirement according to which very powerful but environmentally impactful models (e.g. LLMs) should not be used for simple tasks (e.g. sentiment recognition) when a simpler and performant model is available (e.g. BERT)? If yes, cite which Article or Annex mentions this.
rows.answer: No. Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, as adopted, has no "proportionality of need" rule. No Article or Annex requires providers or deployers to use a smaller model (e.g. BERT) instead of a large language model when the smaller one would do a simple task such as sentiment recognition well enough. The Act regulates AI systems by their intended purpose and risk, and it regulates general-purpose AI models by their capabilities and systemic risk. It does not regulate whether a model is technically necessary for a task. Using an LLM for sentiment analysis is therefore not prohibited under Article 5, and nothing else in the Act forbids it. The environmental provisions stop well short of such a duty. Article 1(1) lists "environmental protection" among the interests the Act protects. This is a statement of purpose and places no duty on anyone to choose a particular model. Article 53(1)(a) requires providers of general-purpose AI models to keep up-to-date technical documentation containing at least the information in Annex XI. Annex XI includes the computing resources used for training and the model's known or estimated energy consumption. This duty only requires providers to record and disclose these figures. It does not limit how the model is used, and deployers have no matching duty. Article 40(2) requires the Commission's standardisation requests to cover deliverables on reporting and documentation that improve resource performance. Examples are lower energy and resource use by high-risk AI systems over their lifecycle, and energy-efficient development of general-purpose AI models. Standards only give a presumption of conformity under Article 40(1). They do not create duties to minimise which model is used. Article 112(6) requires the Commission to report by 2 August 2028, and every four years after that, on progress in standardisation for energy-efficient development of general-purpose AI models. The report must also assess whether further measures, "including binding measures or actions", are needed. This confirms that the adopted text contains no binding efficiency or model-sufficiency rule. The question is left for a future review. A requirement like the one you describe could only come from a future amendment after that review, or from sources outside the AI Act.
criteria_text: No
No provision conditions use of a capable model on unavailability of a simpler/less resource-intensive alternative for the same task
Obligations are risk- and capability-based (e.g. Article 6, Annex III, Article 51), not tied to model right-sizing or environmental impact

rows.question: Article 9 of the AI Act lists the five categories of harm that map to AI systems with: no risk, limited risk, high-risk, systemic risk, prohibited. What are the five categories and how do they map to the five risk levels?
rows.answer: Article 9 contains no list of five harm categories, and it does not map harms to five risk levels. Article 9 is the risk-management duty for high-risk AI systems only. Article 9(1) requires a risk management system to be "established, implemented, documented and maintained in relation to high-risk AI systems". The only kinds of harm it names are risks to "health, safety or fundamental rights" (Article 9(2)(a)). Article 9(3) narrows these to risks "which may be reasonably mitigated or eliminated through the development or design of the high-risk AI system, or the provision of adequate technical information". "Risk" itself is defined in Article 3(2) as "the combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm". The five-level scale in the question ("no risk, limited risk, high-risk, systemic risk, prohibited") is a commentary shorthand, not a structure found in the Regulation. Where each part actually comes from. Prohibited: Article 5(1) bans eight practices outright. (a) subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm; (b) exploiting vulnerabilities due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation; (c) social scoring; (d) criminal-risk profiling based solely on profiling or personality traits; (e) untargeted scraping of facial images; (f) emotion recognition in workplaces and education, except for medical or safety reasons; (g) biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes; (h) real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement, subject to the exceptions in points (h)(i) to (iii). These bans do not depend on any Article 9 assessment. High-risk: this status comes from Article 6 and the listed uses in Annex III, not from Article 9. Article 7(1)(b) lets the Commission add Annex III use cases that pose "a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights" at least equal to existing entries. Only systems classified this way must meet Article 9 and the other Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, such as Articles 10 and 13. Systemic risk: this applies to general-purpose AI models, not AI systems, so it is a separate track rather than a step above high-risk. A model is classified under Article 51(1) if it has high-impact capabilities or the Commission designates it using Annex XIII. High-impact capabilities are presumed above 10^25 FLOPs of training compute (Article 51(2)). Such providers must also meet the Article 55(1)(a) to (d) duties. Article 3(65) defines systemic risk by its effects on "public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, or the society as a whole". That five-item list may be the source of the idea of "five categories", but it describes only systemic risk and maps to no risk tiers. "Limited risk": this is not a statutory term. It usually refers to the Article 50 transparency duties for certain AI systems, such as systems that interact with people directly. "No" or "minimal" risk: this is not a statutory category either. It is simply every AI system that does not fall under Articles 5, 6 or 50, and the Regulation sets no separate risk-management duty for it.
criteria_text: No
Article 9 only establishes the risk management system for high-risk AI systems, not a five-tier harm classification

Four steps: identify/analyze risks (9(2)(a)); estimate/evaluate risks under intended use and foreseeable misuse (9(2)(b)); evaluate risks from post-market monitoring data (9(2)(c)); adopt targeted risk management measures (9(2)(d))
The prohibited/high-risk/limited-risk/minimal-risk/systemic-risk tiering comes from elsewhere in the Regulation (e.g. Articles 5, 6, 50, 51), not Article 9

rows.question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
rows.answer: Yes, the operator can go ahead with the new use, and the AI Act does not require the operator to keep logs for that use. This holds only if the operator's legal team is right that the new use falls under neither Annex I nor Annex III. Three limits apply. Why the high-risk rules don't follow the new use. Under Article 6, whether a system is high-risk depends on what it is used for. There are two routes. Annex I route (Article 6(1)): the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the laws listed in Annex I. The route applies only if both parts of Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are met: the product is covered, and that product must pass a third-party conformity assessment. Annex III route (Article 6(2)): the use matches one of the specific numbered use cases listed in Annex III, not just its general area. If neither route applies, the new use is not high-risk. That means the requirements of Chapter III Section 2 under Article 8 do not apply to it, including. Risk management (Article 9). Data governance (Article 10). Technical documentation (Article 11). Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Article 15). Because Annex III does not apply at all, the Article 6(3) exemption test and its profiling override are not relevant either. Why you don't become the provider. Changing a system's use can make you its provider, but only in the cases listed in Article 25(1), and none fits here. Article 25(1)(c) applies only when a system that was not high-risk is turned into a high-risk one. Article 25(1)(b) applies only when a substantial modification leaves the system still high-risk. Moving a high-risk system to a use that is not high-risk triggers neither. The logging requirement in Article 12(1) says high-risk AI systems must technically allow events to be recorded automatically over their lifetime. It is part of the high-risk regime, so it does not extend to a use outside that regime. The three limits. The operator's existing high-risk use is unaffected. If you keep using the system for its original purpose, all the operator's deployer duties for that use still apply. These include following the provider's instructions for use and keeping the automatically generated logs. So don't switch off or delete logging on a shared instance, or you may breach those duties for the original use. Stay within the intended use as originally framed by the operator's lawyers. If the new use later touches a listed Annex III use case, the system is high-risk again. By changing its intended purpose, you would then become its provider under Article 25(1) and take on the full provider obligations. Get the classification in writing. Record the legal team's Annex I and Annex III analysis before you start. Whether all of the above holds depends entirely on that assessment being correct.
criteria_text: No, cannot proceed with the new use
Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use; deviating from intended use is not excused merely because that use alone wouldn't trigger Annex III
Yes, logging duty under Article 26(6) still applies regardless of the particular use
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states 'Yes, the operator can go ahead with the new use,' which contradicts the correct verdict 'No, cannot proceed with the new use.' The answer incorrectly asserts that deviating from intended use is permissible if the new use is not high-risk, failing to recognize that deployers must use high-risk systems in accordance with instructions for use under Article 26(1), regardless of the risk level of the new use.

The candidate answer does not state that Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use and that deviation is not excused merely because the new use is not high-risk. Instead, it claims the high-risk rules do not apply if Annex I or III do not apply, thereby misrepresenting the scope of deployer obligations under Article 26(1).

The candidate answer incorrectly states that the logging requirement does not apply to the new use because it is outside the high-risk regime. However, Article 26(6) imposes a logging duty on deployers of high-risk AI systems to the extent logs are under their control, regardless of the particular use. The system remains a high-risk AI system, so the logging obligation persists for as long as the deployer controls logs from that system.

rows.question: Is an AI that transcribes doctor-patient conversations prohibited? Or is it high-risk as per the use cases of Annex III of the AI Act?
rows.answer: No, it is not prohibited, and it is not high-risk under Annex III. A standard AI system that transcribes doctor-patient conversations only becomes high-risk through the separate Annex I product route under Article 6(1). Not prohibited. The list of banned practices in Article 5(1)(a), (h) is complete, and turning speech into text fits none of them. The eight banned practices are. Manipulative or deceptive techniques. Exploiting people's vulnerabilities. Social scoring. Predicting criminal offences based solely on profiling. Untargeted scraping of facial images. Emotion recognition in workplaces and education institutions. Biometric categorisation to infer sensitive traits. Real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement. This changes only if the system does more than transcribe. For example, if it infers the clinician's emotions at work, that falls under Article 5(1)(f), which has an exception for medical or safety reasons. Not high-risk under Annex III. Article 6(2) makes a system high-risk only if it falls within an Annex III use case. None of the eight areas covers clinical documentation or transcription. The two healthcare-related entries cover different things. Annex III, point 5(a): public authorities assessing eligibility for public benefits, including healthcare services. Annex III, point 5(d): assessing emergency calls and emergency patient triage. Annex III, point 1(c) (emotion recognition) applies only if the system infers emotions from biometric data. Because the system is outside Annex III, the Article 6(3) exemption for Annex III systems is irrelevant, including its rule that systems profiling people are always high-risk. The product route under Article 6(1). Separately, the system is high-risk if both of these are true. It is a product, or a safety component of a product, covered by the EU laws listed in Annex I. Here that means the Medical Devices Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (Annex I, point 11) or the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (Annex I, point 12). That product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment. Pure transcription for record-keeping normally has no medical purpose, so it is not a medical device. It could qualify if it also. Extracts diagnoses, suggests treatment, or. Otherwise supports clinical decisions, and it would then be high-risk if its device class requires a notified body assessment. Transparency. Article 50 may still apply. The provider must tell people they are dealing with AI only if the system interacts directly with them, unless that is obvious. AI-generated text must be marked in a machine-readable way. This does not apply where the system only assists standard editing or does not substantially change the input or its meaning, which a faithful transcript generally does not. AI-written summaries or clinical notes may fall outside that exception.
criteria_text: No, not a prohibited practice under Article 5
No, not high-risk under Annex III
Reason: narrow procedural task derogation, Article 6(3), point (a)

rows.question: As a deployer, do I need to keep logs if I use a powerful LLM (surpassing the FLOPs threshold) for estimating whether customer payment confirmations are received via email?
rows.answer: No. The AI Act does not require you, as a deployer, to keep logs for this use. The model being a systemic-risk general-purpose AI model does not change that. Who the systemic-risk rules apply to. Under Article 51(1)(a) and 51(2), a general-purpose AI model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities if its cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs. That classification sets obligations for the provider of the model. Article 3(3) defines the provider as whoever develops the model and places it on the market. It does not set obligations for someone who uses a system built on the model. You use the system under the operator's authority, so the operator is a deployer under Article 3(4). The system is a "general-purpose AI system" under Article 3(66). The Regulation gives deployers no record-keeping or log-retention duty just because the underlying model has systemic risk. Why the deployer log duty does not apply. Deployers must keep automatically generated logs only for high-risk AI systems. Under Article 6, a system is high-risk only if it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product under the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I, or if it is used for one of the listed high-risk use cases. Checking whether a customer's payment confirmation has arrived by email is neither. It is an ordinary back-office task, so the system is not high-risk and you have no log-keeping duty under the AI Act. When the operator's role could change. Under Article 25(1)(c), you would become the provider of a high-risk AI system only if you changed the system's intended purpose so that it became high-risk under Article 6. An example would be using the payment outputs to assess the creditworthiness of natural persons. You would then take on the provider obligations. Separately, the Commission's 18 July 2025 guidelines on general-purpose AI models make you a new model provider if you modify the model with more than one-third of its original training compute. If that compute is unknown, the threshold is one-third of 10^25 FLOPs, about 3.3×10^24 FLOPs. Those model-level duties still would not create a deployer log-keeping duty for this use. Other laws, such as data-protection or accounting rules, may still require the operator to keep records.

Article 26(6) logging duty applies only to deployers of high-risk AI systems
This use case is not a high-risk use case listed in Annex III
FLOPs threshold concerns GPAI systemic-risk classification under Article 51, a separate regime irrelevant to Annex III high-risk classification

rows.question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
rows.answer: Yes. AI software that helps clinicians choose the best treatment is potentially high-risk. The route is Article 6(1) read with Annex I (points 11 and 12). Annex III is not the route. Annex I lists Union harmonisation legislation, including Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices (point 11) and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices (point 12). Under the MDR, software intended to provide information used to make diagnostic or therapeutic decisions is itself a medical device. Article 6(1) makes an AI system high-risk, "irrespective of whether [it] is placed on the market or put into service independently" of the products in points (a) and (b), when both of these conditions are met. Condition (a): the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, or is itself such a product. Condition (b): that product, or the product it is a safety component of, must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation before it is placed on the market or put into service. When condition (b) is met. Under MDR classification Rule 11, software that supports diagnostic or therapeutic decisions is at least class IIa. It is class IIb if a decision could seriously worsen a patient's health or lead to surgery. It is class III if a decision could cause death or an irreversible worsening of health. All of these classes need a notified body, so condition (b) will normally be met and the system is high-risk. Only software that qualifies as a class I device, with no notified body involved, would fall outside Article 6(1). Why Annex III does not apply. Article 6(2) and Annex III cover only listed uses. None of them covers clinical treatment decisions in general. The health-related entries are narrow. Point 5(a): public authorities assessing eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services. Point 5(c): risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance. Point 5(d): emergency healthcare patient triage systems. The system would be caught under Annex III only if it were actually used for one of those purposes. The Article 6(3) exemption does not help. Article 6(3) lets a system escape high-risk status if it performs a narrow procedural task, improves a completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns, or performs a preparatory task. That exemption applies only to Annex III systems. It cannot be used for an AI medical device that is high-risk under Article 6(1). Conformity assessment. Under Article 43(3), the device goes through the MDR/IVDR notified-body procedure, which also checks the AI Act's high-risk requirements. Those requirements include the risk management system in Article 9, which lines up with ISO 14971.

Article 6(2)
Annex III (healthcare access/provision)

rows.question: Is irregular migration a topic considered in the AI Act? If so, to what risk category does it belong?
rows.answer: Yes. Irregular migration is expressly covered by the AI Act, and AI systems used to assess it are high-risk. Annex III, point 7 covers "Migration, asylum and border control management, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law". Under point 7(b), this includes AI systems used by or on behalf of competent public authorities, or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, to assess a risk posed by a natural person who intends to enter, or has entered, the territory of a Member State. The listed risks are a security risk, a risk of irregular migration and a health risk. Point 7 lists three other related uses. 7(a): polygraphs or similar tools. 7(c): helping authorities examine applications for asylum, visa or residence permits, and related complaints. This includes assessing how reliable the evidence is. 7(d): detecting, recognising or identifying natural persons in the context of migration, asylum or border control management. Verifying travel documents is excluded. Article 6(2) says AI systems listed in Annex III are high-risk. This is separate from the Annex I product route in Article 6(1). Exception. Under Article 6(3), an Annex III system is not high-risk if it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights. This includes not materially influencing the outcome of decisions. At least one of these conditions must also be met. (a) it performs a narrow procedural task; (b) it improves the result of a human activity that has already been completed; (c) it detects decision-making patterns, or departures from earlier patterns, and is not meant to replace or influence the completed human assessment without proper human review; (d) it performs a preparatory task for an assessment relevant to an Annex III use case. The exception never applies if the system profiles natural persons. Such a system is always high-risk. Individual risk assessments under point 7(b) will often involve profiling. A provider that relies on the exception must document its assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service. It must also register under Article 49(2) and give the documentation to national competent authorities on request (Article 6(4)). Duty for deployers. Under Article 27(1), deployers that are bodies governed by public law, or private entities providing public services, must carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use. In practice this covers migration and border authorities using these systems. The assessment must describe. (a) the processes in which the system will be used; (b) how long and how often it will be used; (c) the categories of people affected; (d) the specific risks of harm to them; (e) the human oversight measures; (f) the measures to take if those risks materialise, including internal governance and complaint mechanisms. The deployer must update the assessment if these elements change (Article 27(2)). It must notify the market surveillance authority of the results using the template, unless the Article 46(1) exemption applies (Article 27(3)). The assessment complements any data protection impact assessment already done under the GDPR or Directive (EU) 2016/680 (Article 27(4)).

rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
rows.answer: Under Article 53(1)(b) and Annex XII, a provider of a general-purpose AI model must give AI system providers who plan to integrate it the following. Date of release: Yes. Annex XII, point 1(c), requires "the date of release and methods of distribution.". Number of parameters: Yes. Annex XII, point 1(f), requires "the architecture and number of parameters.". How the model interacts with hardware: Yes, where applicable. Annex XII, point 1(d), requires a description of "how the model interacts, or can be used to interact, with hardware or software that is not part of the model itself, where applicable.". Licence: Yes. Annex XII, point 1(h), requires "the licence for the model.". Samples of outlier data used in training: No. Annex XII, point 2(c), only requires "information on the data used for training, testing and validation, where applicable, including the type and provenance of data and curation methodologies." It does not require samples of training data, outliers or otherwise. Annex IV, point 2(d), mentions outlier detection, but only as a data-cleaning method in high-risk AI system documentation. It does not apply to disclosures to downstream providers. The public training-content summary under Article 53(1)(d) does not require data samples either. Annex XII sets the minimum. Under Article 53(1)(b)(i), the information must also give downstream providers a good understanding of the model's capabilities and limitations. It must also let them meet their own obligations under the Regulation. Under Article 53(1)(b), all of this is without prejudice to protecting intellectual property rights, confidential business information and trade secrets under Union and national law. Open-source exception: Under Article 53(2), the Article 53(1)(b) duty does not apply to models released under a free and open-source licence that allows access, use, modification and distribution. The model's parameters, including weights, architecture information and model usage information, must also be publicly available. This exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk under Article 51.

rows.question: Who, if at all, needs to establish the post-market monitoring system for a high-risk AI system? Provider/deployer/AI office? Is it possible that the monitoring system may need to also include info on interaction with other AI systems than the high-risk one in consideration?
rows.answer: Only the provider has to establish the post-market monitoring system. Neither the deployer nor the AI Office does. And yes, where relevant, the system must also cover how the high-risk AI system interacts with other AI systems. Who is responsible. Article 72(1) puts the duty on providers. They must "establish and document a post-market monitoring system" in a way that is proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the high-risk AI system. The duty is also part of the provider's quality management system: Article 17(1)(h) requires that system to include "the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system, in accordance with Article 72". Under Article 72(3), the system must be based on a post-market monitoring plan. That plan forms part of the provider's technical documentation. The Commission (not the AI Office) was to adopt an implementing act setting out a template for the plan. Article 72(4) adds a simplification. Providers of high-risk AI systems covered by Annex I Section A legislation that already requires a monitoring system and plan may build the required elements into those existing systems. The same applies to certain regulated financial institutions. Role of deployers. Deployers do not establish the system. Under Article 72(2), they are a source of the data it collects: the system gathers relevant data "which may be provided by deployers or which may be collected through other sources". A deployer does take on the full duty if Article 25(1) makes it a provider. That happens if it. Puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service; makes a substantial modification after which the system remains high-risk; or. Changes the intended purpose of a system so that it becomes high-risk. The same rule applies to distributors, importers and other third parties. Role of the AI Office. The AI Office has no duty to establish or run a post-market monitoring system for high-risk AI systems. Interaction with other AI systems. Article 72(2) requires the system to "actively and systematically collect, document and analyse" relevant data on the system's performance throughout its lifetime. The purpose is to let the provider check that the system continues to meet the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements. The same paragraph says expressly: "Where relevant, post-market monitoring shall include an analysis of the interaction with other AI systems.". This is not optional, but it depends on relevance. It applies where interactions with other AI systems could affect performance or compliance. Two other provisions support this reading. High-risk AI systems must be as resilient as possible to errors, faults or inconsistencies, "in particular due to their interaction with natural persons or other systems". The risk management system must evaluate other risks that emerge from analysing post-market monitoring data. Where other AI systems, tools or components are built into the high-risk system, Article 25(4) helps the provider get the information it needs. The provider and the third-party supplier must set out in a written agreement the necessary information, capabilities, technical access and other assistance. This does not apply to third parties that make tools, services, processes or components (other than general-purpose AI models) publicly available under a free and open-source licence. Exception. Under Article 72(2), the monitoring duty does not cover sensitive operational data of deployers that are law-enforcement authorities.

Not deployer or AI Office
Yes — must include analysis of interaction with other AI systems where relevant

rows.question: What is an "area" and what is a "use case" for high-risk as per Article 6(2)? How many areas exist?
rows.answer: Under Article 6(2), an area is one of the numbered headings of Annex III, and a use case is a specific intended purpose listed under that heading. There are eight areas. What makes a system high-risk under Article 6(2) is the use case, not the area alone. Each area is a broad field of activity. The Act itself uses this word: Article 7(1)(a) refers to "areas listed in Annex III", Article 27(1) to "the area listed in point 2 of Annex III", and Article 112(2)(a) to "area headings". The eight areas are. Biometrics, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law. Critical infrastructure. Education and vocational training. Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment. Access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits. Law enforcement, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law. Migration, asylum and border control management, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law. Administration of justice and democratic processes. Use case. A use case describes a particular AI system by what it is intended to do. Examples are Annex III point 5(b), creditworthiness assessment or credit scoring (financial-fraud detection excluded), and point 5(c), risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance. Most use cases are lettered points under an area. Point 2 is the exception: it has no lettered points, and its single use case sits in the heading itself (safety components in managing and operating critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity). As adopted, Annex III contains 25 use cases. 3 in area 1. 1 in area 2. 4 in area 3. 2 in area 4. 4 in area 5. 5 in area 6. 4 in area 7. 2 in area 8. Why the difference matters. A system is high-risk under Article 6(2) only if its intended purpose matches a listed use case. Working in a listed area is not enough. Derogation. Even then, Article 6(3) lets the system escape high-risk status if it poses no significant risk of harm and meets one of four conditions: a narrow procedural task, improving a completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing human assessment, or a preparatory task. A system that profiles natural persons is always high-risk. Adding or changing use cases. Under Article 7(1), the Commission can add or modify use cases by delegated act only if both conditions are met: the system is used in an area already listed, and its risk is equivalent to or greater than that of existing Annex III systems. Article 7(3) governs removing use cases. Adding or extending areas. This cannot be done by delegated act. The Commission evaluates the need under Article 112(2)(a), and any change requires amending the Regulation.

Use case = specific application listed within an area (lettered sub-point)
8 areas exist

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: No, healthcare decision-making is not one of the high-risk areas. Annex III lists eight areas, and none is "healthcare". Some health-related uses are still high-risk, either because they are listed use-cases inside another area or because they fall under the separate Annex I product route. The eight Annex III areas (Article 6(2), Annex III points 1 to 8). Biometrics, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law. Critical infrastructure. Education and vocational training. Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment. Access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits. Law enforcement, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law. Migration, asylum and border control management, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law. Administration of justice and democratic processes. A system is only high-risk under this route if it matches a specific use-case listed under one of these areas. Health-related use-cases that are listed. Annex III point 5(a): systems used by or on behalf of public authorities to judge whether people are eligible for essential public assistance benefits and services, "including healthcare services". This also covers granting, reducing, revoking or reclaiming them. Annex III point 5(c): systems used for risk assessment and pricing of natural persons in life and health insurance. Annex III point 5(d): systems that evaluate and classify emergency calls, dispatch or prioritise emergency first responders (including medical aid), and emergency healthcare patient triage systems. Annex III point 7(b): systems used by or on behalf of competent public authorities or Union bodies to assess a health risk posed by a person who intends to enter, or has entered, a Member State. Clinical decision-making tools, such as diagnostic or treatment-support software, usually come in through Annex I instead. Under Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk if both of these apply. It is a product, or a safety component of a product, covered by Annex I, which includes the medical devices regulation (EU) 2017/745 (point 11) and the in vitro diagnostic medical devices regulation (EU) 2017/746 (point 12); and. That product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. The Article 6(3) exception applies only to Annex III systems, not Annex I. An Annex III system is not high-risk if it poses no significant risk of harm and meets one of four conditions. It performs a narrow procedural task; it improves the result of a human activity already completed; it detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the earlier human assessment without proper human review; or. It performs a preparatory task for an Annex III assessment. This exception never applies if the system profiles natural persons. The Commission cannot add healthcare as a new area. Under Article 7(1), in accordance with Article 97, it can only add or modify use-cases within the existing Annex III areas. Both conditions must be met: the use falls within a listed area, and its risk is equivalent to or greater than that of the high-risk systems already listed.

No

rows.question: What does Annex VII point 5.1 say? Try to get the substance right. Do not get confused with other material, like 5.1 in Annex III or Article 7, which is about something else entirely.
rows.answer: Annex VII point 5.1 says that the notified body's surveillance exists to make sure the provider duly complies with the terms and conditions of the quality management system (QMS) it approved. It is the first sub-point of point 5, "Surveillance of the approved quality management system". The surveillance is carried out by the notified body referred to in point 3, which is the body that assessed and approved the provider's QMS. Point 5.1 only states what surveillance is for. It is the step that point 2 of Annex VII refers to when it says the approved QMS for the design, development and testing of AI systems under Article 17 is examined under point 3 "and shall be subject to surveillance as specified in point 5.". The rest of point 5 sets out how surveillance works. Point 5.2: the provider must let the notified body into the premises where the AI systems are designed, developed and tested, and must share all necessary information. Point 5.3: the notified body must carry out periodic audits to check that the provider keeps up and applies the QMS, and must give the provider an audit report. During those audits it may run additional tests on AI systems that hold a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. This is a different provision from Annex III point 5, which lists high-risk uses around essential private and public services. It is also unrelated to Article 7, which covers the Commission's power to amend Annex III.

rows.question: Do providers of GPAI systems, even if not with systemic risk, have an obligation to extensively shield their models from adversarial attacks? What about specifically for adversarial images? What about specifically for prompt injection?
rows.answer: No. A provider of a general-purpose AI model without systemic risk has no obligation under the AI Act to shield the model from adversarial attacks, extensively or otherwise. Such a provider's duties are listed in Article 53(1), and there are only four. Keep technical documentation up to date, per Annex XI (point (a)); give information and documentation to downstream providers who build the model into their AI systems (point (b)); have a policy for complying with EU copyright law (point (c)); publish a summary of the content used for training (point (d)). Under Article 53(2), points (a) and (b) do not apply to models released under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters. None of the four duties requires robustness, adversarial testing or cybersecurity. The closest link is Article 53(1)(b)(i). The downstream information must let integrators understand "the capabilities and limitations" of the model. That is a duty to disclose, not a duty to harden the model. Security duties for general-purpose AI models apply only once the model has systemic risk under Article 51. Under Article 51(2), that is presumed above 10^25 FLOPs of training compute. Under Article 51(1)(b), the Commission can also designate a model. For these models, Article 55(1)(a) requires "conducting and documenting adversarial testing," but only "with a view to identifying and mitigating systemic risks." Article 55(1)(d) requires "an adequate level of cybersecurity protection" for the model and its physical infrastructure. Even here the test is adequacy, measured against systemic risk and the state of the art. It is not a duty to block every attack. Under Article 53(4), providers may show compliance by following the Article 56 codes of practice until a harmonised standard is published. Note also that the operator's question refers to general-purpose AI systems. Chapter V places these duties on providers of general-purpose AI models (Article 3(63)), not systems (Article 3(66)). A general-purpose AI system has its own robustness duty only if it is, or becomes, a high-risk AI system. Under Article 25(1)(c), whoever changes its intended purpose so that it becomes high-risk is treated as its provider. Adversarial images: The Act names "inputs designed to cause the AI model to make a mistake (adversarial examples or model evasion)" only in Article 15(5), and only for high-risk AI systems. Even there, measures are needed "where appropriate" and must be "appropriate to the relevant circumstances and the risks." That duty falls on the provider of the high-risk system, not on the upstream model provider. For a model without systemic risk, adversarial images create no specific duty. For a model with systemic risk, they are covered only to the extent they are relevant to systemic risks under Article 55(1)(a) and (d). Prompt injection: The Act does not name prompt injection anywhere. For high-risk AI systems, it is covered in substance by Article 15(5). The system must be "resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities." The listed countermeasures include measures against adversarial examples and "model flaws." For a model with systemic risk, prompt injection is covered by the adversarial testing in Article 55(1)(a) and the cybersecurity duty in Article 55(1)(d), again limited to systemic risk. For a model without systemic risk, there is no statutory duty to prevent it. One indirect route does exist. When a model is built into a high-risk AI system, Article 25(4) requires the model supplier and the high-risk provider to agree in writing on the information, capabilities and technical access the high-risk provider needs to comply, including with Article 15. Unlike other free and open-source components, general-purpose AI models are not exempt from this. The robustness duty itself still rests with the high-risk system's provider.
