Applies only to GPAI models with systemic risk, under Article 55(1)(a)
Adversarial images not separately addressed - only general adversarial-testing duty
Prompt injection not separately addressed - not mentioned in Article 55

The answer states that adversarial images are not separately addressed in the Act for GPAI models, only covered under the general adversarial-testing duty for systemic-risk models.
The answer confirms that prompt injection is not mentioned in Article 55 and explains its coverage only by implication under systemic risk provisions.

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No. Adding guardrails to an agentic AI system does not move it out of the high-risk category, and the AI Act has no "moderate risk" category to move it into. Changing the system's intended purpose, and the functions it actually performs, can change its classification. Why guardrails don't change the classification. Under Article 6 there are only two ways a system becomes high-risk, and neither depends on how much risk is left after mitigation. Annex III route (Article 6(2)): the system's intended use falls within one of the lettered use-cases listed under the eight Annex III areas. Annex I route (Article 6(1)): the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Annex I legislation, and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment. Guardrails change neither of these facts. Legally, they are risk-management and risk-control measures: the "targeted" measures under Article 9(2)(d), tested under Article 9(5), with the remaining risk judged acceptable and communicated to the deployer under Article 9(6). Article 8(1) makes them part of how a high-risk system meets the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, not a way out of them. They must also be described in the instructions for use: capabilities and limitations, and foreseeable circumstances that could lead to risk (Article 13(3)(b)(ii), (iii)). The Article 6(3) exception. For Annex III systems, the one route out is Article 6(3). A system is not high-risk if it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, and it meets at least one of four conditions. (a) it performs a narrow procedural task; (b) it improves the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) it detects decision-making patterns or deviations from them, and is not meant to replace or influence the completed human assessment without proper human review; (d) it performs a preparatory task for an assessment relevant to an Annex III use-case. This exception never applies if the system profiles natural persons; such a system is always high-risk. A provider relying on the exception must document its assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service. It also remains subject to registration and must give the documentation to national competent authorities on request (Article 6(4)). Guardrails help here only if they genuinely confine what the system does to one of conditions (a), (d). At that point, what has really changed is the system's function, not just its safety layer. Mitigation also appears in Article 7(2)(k)(ii), but that concerns measures provided by existing Union law. It is one of the criteria the Commission weighs when changing Annex III by delegated act (Article 7(1) and (3), Article 97). It does not let a provider reclassify its own system. Why changing intended purpose and capabilities can work. Under Article 6(2), classification depends on the intended purpose. If the agent is redesigned so that it no longer performs a listed use-case, it falls outside the high-risk category. Examples would be no longer screening job candidates, allocating tasks to workers or evaluating access to essential services. Alternatively, it can be narrowed so that it qualifies under Article 6(3). The declared purpose must be backed up in practice. It must be stated in the instructions for use (Article 13(3)(b)(i)). It should be supported by actually removing the relevant capabilities, such as tool access, decision authority or profiling functions. Merely telling users not to use the system that way is weak. Risks from reasonably foreseeable misuse remain relevant (Article 9(2)(b)). For Annex I systems, only changing the product or its safety-component role changes the outcome. The reverse risk. Changing a system's purpose can also create high-risk status and shift obligations. A distributor, importer, deployer or other third party who changes the intended purpose of a non-high-risk system (including a general-purpose AI system) so that it becomes high-risk is treated as its provider, with all Article 16 obligations (Article 25(1)(c)). The same applies to anyone who makes a substantial modification to a high-risk system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Duties that remain after reclassification. Leaving the high-risk category does not remove every obligation. Disclosure (Article 50(1)): an agent that interacts directly with people must tell them they are dealing with AI. This does not apply where that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person. It also does not apply to systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, unless the public can use them to report a crime. Content marking (Article 50(2)): synthetic output must be marked in a machine-readable, detectable format. Timing (Article 50(5)): this information must be given clearly at the latest at the first interaction or exposure. Underlying model: if the agent is built on a general-purpose AI model, the model provider's Article 53 obligations are unaffected. Any systemic-risk classification under Article 51 depends on the model's own capabilities or training compute, not on guardrails added at the system level.
criteria_text: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes

The answer confirms that changing the system's intended purpose and capabilities can remove high-risk status if the new purpose meets one of the Article 6(3) conditions.

rows.question: Can law enforcement starts using a real-time remote biometric identification system without prior authorisation? If yes, how much time do they have to seek authorisation, and what happens if the authorisation is refused?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 5(3), law enforcement can start using a "real-time" remote biometric identification system in publicly accessible spaces without prior authorisation, but only in a duly justified situation of urgency. Authorisation must then be requested without undue delay and within 24 hours at the latest. If it is refused, use must stop immediately and all data, results and outputs of that use must be deleted at once. The normal rule. Under Article 5(3), each such use needs prior authorisation. The authorisation comes from a judicial authority, or an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding, in the Member State where the use takes place. It is issued on a reasoned request and under the detailed national rules in Article 5(5). Use is only lawful at all where a Member State has chosen to allow it in national law under Article 5(5). It must also be strictly necessary for one of the three objectives in Article 5(1)(h). The targeted search for specific victims of abduction, human trafficking or sexual exploitation, or for missing persons; preventing a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, or a genuine and present or foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack; finding or identifying a person suspected of an Annex II offence punishable in that Member State by a maximum custodial sentence or detention order of at least four years. The urgency exception. Deadline: Under Article 5(3), authorisation must be requested without undue delay, at the latest within 24 hours. Related urgency rule: Under Article 5(2), use normally also requires a completed fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and registration in the EU database under Article 49. In duly justified urgent cases, use may start before registration, provided registration is completed without undue delay. If authorisation is refused. Under Article 5(3). Use must stop with immediate effect; all the data, and all results and outputs of that use, must be discarded and deleted immediately. How the authority decides. It may grant authorisation only if objective evidence or clear indications show the use is necessary and proportionate for the objective in the request. The use must be limited to what is strictly necessary in time, geographic scope and the persons covered. The authority must also weigh the factors in Article 5(2): the nature of the situation and the consequences for the rights and freedoms of the people concerned. Other safeguards. No decision with an adverse legal effect on a person may be based solely on the system's output (Article 5(3)). Each use must be notified to the relevant market surveillance authority and national data protection authority, without sensitive operational data (Article 5(4)). Don't confuse this with Article 46(2). Article 46(2) is a separate urgency rule for putting a high-risk AI system into service without the market surveillance authority's conformity-assessment authorisation. It has no 24-hour limit. On refusal, it requires use to stop and results and outputs to be discarded. It does not replace the Article 5(3) regime for real-time remote biometric identification.

Authorisation must be requested without undue delay, at the latest within 24 hours
If refused: use stopped immediately, all data/results/outputs discarded and deleted

The answer explicitly states that authorisation must be requested without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours, satisfying criterion 2.
The answer clearly states that if authorisation is refused, use must stop immediately and all data, results, and outputs must be deleted at once, which matches the requirement in criterion 3.

rows.question: Consider a private contractor of the municipality that runs a city's emergency-call triage platform. The contractor plans to use an AI tool to prioritize police response decisions. Before going live with the system, does this contractor need to look into fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA)? Is this because of this scenario belonging to Annex III 5(b) or 5(c)? What about private contractors offering other public services concerning Annex III but NOT specifically 5(b) or 5(c)?
rows.answer: Yes, the contractor must carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA) before going live. But the duty does not come from Annex III point 5(b) or 5(c). It applies because the contractor is a private entity providing public services, and it deploys a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2). Annex III point 5(d) covers AI systems "intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls by natural persons or to be used to dispatch, or to establish priority in the dispatching of, emergency first response services, including by police." An AI tool that prioritises police response on an emergency-call triage platform fits that entry, so it is high-risk under Article 6(2). The Article 6(3) exception is unlikely to help. It removes high-risk status only if the system poses no significant risk of harm and does not materially influence decisions. It must also meet one of four conditions: a narrow procedural task, improving a completed human activity, detecting patterns without replacing human assessment, or a preparatory task. Setting police dispatch priority directly shapes the outcome, so it is hard to call it narrow or preparatory. If the system profiles natural persons, it is always high-risk. Why 5(b) and 5(c) are not the reason. Those points cover. 5(b): assessing creditworthiness or setting credit scores, except fraud detection. 5(c): risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance. Under Article 27(1), those two uses trigger a FRIA for every deployer, even a purely private one serving private customers. That is a separate, additional trigger. The contractor's duty comes from the other limb of Article 27(1): deployers that are "bodies governed by public law, or are private entities providing public services." Running a city's emergency-call triage on behalf of the municipality is a public service. The contractor uses the system under its own authority, so it is the deployer. What the FRIA must contain under Article 27(1)(a), (f). A description of the deployer's processes where the system is used, in line with its intended purpose; the period of time and how often the system will be used; the categories of people and groups likely to be affected; the specific risks of harm to those groups, using the provider's information under Article 13; how human oversight measures are implemented, following the instructions for use; the steps to take if those risks materialise, including internal governance and complaint mechanisms. Other duties under Article 27. The assessment is required before first use. It may reuse earlier assessments in similar cases and must be updated if any element changes. The results must be notified to the market surveillance authority. Where a data protection impact assessment (under GDPR Article 35 or Directive 2016/680 Article 27) already covers some elements, the FRIA complements it. The AI Office will provide a template. Other private contractors providing public services. The same rule applies to any Annex III area, not just 5(b) or 5(c). A private entity providing public services must do a FRIA before deploying any Article 6(2) high-risk system. That includes. Biometrics (area 1); education and vocational training (area 3); employment and workers' management (area 4); point 5(a) public assistance eligibility, and point 5(d); law enforcement (area 6); migration, asylum and border control (area 7); administration of justice and democratic processes (area 8). Exceptions. Critical infrastructure (Annex III area 2) is excluded, even when a private contractor runs it as a public service. Examples are road traffic management and the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity. No FRIA is needed where the system is not high-risk because the Article 6(3) exception validly applies. A private deployer that does not provide public services needs a FRIA only for 5(b) or 5(c) systems.
criteria_text: Yes, FRIA required
No — trigger is being a "private entity providing public services" under Article 27(1), not Annex III 5(b)/(c)
5(b)/(c) is a separate, additional limb pulling in deployers of those specific systems even when not providing public services
Other private contractors offering public services outside 5(b)/(c) remain covered via the general public-service limb, for every Annex III area except point 2
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that the contractor must carry out a FRIA, satisfying the 'Yes, FRIA required' criterion.

The answer clearly explains that the obligation arises because the contractor is a private entity providing public services, not because of Annex III 5(b) or 5(c), aligning with the substance of the criterion.
The answer identifies that 5(b) and 5(c) create a separate, additional obligation applying to all deployers regardless of public service provision, which matches the criterion's substance.

The answer confirms that other private contractors providing public services are covered under the general limb for all Annex III areas except point 2, and explicitly lists examples and excludes critical infrastructure, satisfying the criterion.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, the operator can use them. The EU AI Act does not ban deepfake images for teaching. But if the images count as "deep fakes", the university must disclose that they are AI-generated. Neither the lighter regime nor the law-enforcement carve-out applies to this kind of teaching use. Why the use is allowed. None of the banned practices in Article 5(1) covers making synthetic medical images for teaching. It also isn't high-risk. The education area of Annex III (point 3) covers only its listed uses, such as. Admission to education, evaluating learning outcomes, assessing the level of education someone should receive, monitoring students during tests. Producing illustrations for class is not on that list, so the high-risk rules under Article 6(2) don't apply. When disclosure is required. Article 3(60) defines a "deep fake" as AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that. Resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events, and. Would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful. Lifelike images of skin conditions on what look like real patients will usually meet both parts, because students would take them for genuine clinical photos. A clearly stylised drawing that nobody would mistake for a real photo may fall outside the definition. Where the images are deep fakes, the university is the "deployer" under Article 3(4), since staff use the AI system under its authority in a professional setting. Article 50(4) first subparagraph then requires it to disclose that the content was artificially generated or manipulated. Two related points. The tool's provider must separately mark outputs in a machine-readable, detectable format under Article 50(2). That does not replace the university's own duty. Article 50(2) itself does not apply where the tool only performs an assistive function for standard editing, or does not substantially alter the input or its meaning. If the university builds its own generator, it is also the provider and carries the Article 50(2) duty itself. Why the lighter or exempt regimes don't apply. Law enforcement: for deepfakes, Article 50(4) contains a full exemption, not a lighter duty, and only where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. University teaching is not such a use. Lighter regime: the reduced duty applies only to content in an "evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme". There, it is enough to disclose that such content exists in a way that does not hamper display or enjoyment of the work. Teaching is not on that list. A clinical teaching image is meant to look realistic, not evidently fictional, so it is hard to call it "analogous". Human review: the exemption for content that has undergone human review or editorial control, with someone holding editorial responsibility, covers only AI-generated text published to inform the public. It does not cover deepfake images. How to disclose. Under Article 50(5), the notice must be clear and distinguishable, given at the latest when students first see the content, and meet applicable accessibility requirements. In practice, a visible label on each image or slide, or a clear notice before the images are shown, will do. This doesn't interfere with the teaching. Timing and other law. As adopted, Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026, so it already applies. Under Article 50(6), these duties sit alongside other transparency obligations in EU or national law. If the images were created or adapted from real patient photos, the GDPR's rules on health data apply separately.
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the use is allowed because it does not fall under banned practices or high-risk categories.
The answer explicitly states that disclosure is required under Article 50(4) for deep fakes, which lifelike medical images typically are.
The answer concludes that the lighter regime does not apply because teaching is not analogous to artistic or fictional works, directly contradicting the criterion.
The answer correctly explains that the law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable to university teaching.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose suitable for regulatory guidance, without self-reference or informality.

rows.question: If a high-risk AI system was already placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026, does the AI Act fully apply to it? What about general purpose AI systems?
rows.answer: No, the AI Act does not fully apply to a high-risk AI system placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026. Under Article 111(2), it applies to the operators of such a system only if the system's design undergoes significant changes on or after that date. There are four qualifications. Prohibited practices: Article 111(2) is "without prejudice to" Article 5. Chapters I and II have applied since 2 February 2025 (Article 113(3)(a)). A pre-existing system that carries out a practice banned by Article 5 is therefore covered whether or not it changes. Article 4 on AI literacy, which is in Chapter I, has also applied to providers and deployers since that date. Public authorities: Providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended to be used by public authorities must comply with the Regulation by 2 August 2030 "in any case". This applies even if the system's design never changes. Large-scale EU IT systems: Article 111(2) does not cover systems under Article 111(1). These are AI systems that are components of the large-scale IT systems set up by the acts listed in Annex X (points 1 to 7). The Schengen Information System. The Visa Information System. Eurodac. The Entry/Exit System. ECRIS-TCN. The interoperability Regulations. If such a system was placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2027, it must comply by 31 December 2030. Annex I products: Classification under Article 6(1) and the obligations that go with it apply only from 2 August 2027 (Article 113(3)(c)). The general date of 2 August 2026 is set by Article 113(2). For general-purpose AI, the Act regulates the models, and the transition works differently. Chapter V has applied since 2 August 2025 (Article 113(3)(b)). Under Article 111(3), providers of models placed on the market before that date must take the necessary steps to comply by 2 August 2027. There is no significant-change condition, so these models become fully subject to the Act on that date. From then, the provider must. Technical documentation: draw up and keep up to date the model's technical documentation (Article 53(1)(a)). Information for downstream providers: draw up, keep up to date and make available information and documentation for providers of AI systems that integrate the model (Article 53(1)(b)). Copyright: put in place a copyright policy, including respecting reservations of rights under Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 (Article 53(1)(c)). Training-data summary: make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training (Article 53(1)(d)). Article 53(2) exempts free and open-source models from points (a) and (b), unless the model has systemic risk. A model has systemic risk under Article 51 if it has high-impact capabilities, which are presumed above 10^25 FLOPs of cumulative training compute, or if the Commission designates it. Providers of such models must also meet Article 55(1). Evaluation: evaluate the model, including adversarial testing. Risk mitigation: assess and mitigate systemic risks at Union level. Incidents: track, document and report serious incidents to the AI Office. Cybersecurity: ensure adequate cybersecurity for the model and its physical infrastructure. An AI system built on a general-purpose AI model is treated as an ordinary AI system. If it is high-risk, its transition falls under Article 111(1) or (2), not Article 111(3).
criteria_text: No, does not fully apply
Applies only if system undergoes significant changes in design as from 2 August 2026
High-risk systems for public authorities must comply by 2 August 2030 regardless
GPAI models placed on market before 2 August 2025 must comply by 2 August 2027
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the AI Act does not fully apply to high-risk systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026.
The answer specifies that the Act applies only if the system undergoes significant changes in design on or after 2 August 2026, citing Article 111(2).
The answer clearly states that providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems for public authorities must comply by 2 August 2030 regardless of design changes.
The answer states that GPAI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply by 2 August 2027, referencing Article 111(3).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: What is Annex X about? What is it used for?
rows.answer: Annex X lists the Union legislative acts that set up the EU's large-scale IT systems in the area of Freedom, Security and Justice. It imposes no obligations itself. Its purpose is to identify which AI systems get the special transition period in Article 111(1). The list in Annex X, points 1 to 7, is exhaustive. Schengen Information System (SIS): Regulations (EU) 2018/1860, 2018/1861 and 2018/1862. Visa Information System (VIS): Regulations (EU) 2021/1133 and 2021/1134. Eurodac: Regulation (EU) 2024/1358. Entry/Exit System (EES): Regulation (EU) 2017/2226. European Travel Information and Authorisation System (ETIAS): Regulations (EU) 2018/1240 and 2018/1241. European Criminal Records Information System on third-country nationals and stateless persons (ECRIS-TCN): Regulation (EU) 2019/816. Interoperability framework: Regulations (EU) 2019/817 and 2019/818. The annex matters because of Article 111(1). That provision covers AI systems that are components of the large-scale IT systems set up by these acts. If such a system was placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2027, it must be brought into compliance with the Regulation by 31 December 2030. This extended deadline has two qualifications. Prohibited practices still apply. The deadline is "without prejudice to the application of Article 5 as referred to in Article 113(3), point (a)". The bans in Article 5 therefore apply to these systems without waiting for 2030. Later evaluations must consider the Regulation. Each of these IT systems is evaluated under its own legal act, and when that act is replaced or amended. Those evaluations must take the Regulation's requirements into account. Article 111(2) expressly excludes systems covered by paragraph 1. So the separate transition rule for other high-risk AI systems does not apply to them. That rule covers systems placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026. The Regulation reaches them only after significant design changes, and public-authority systems must comply by 2 August 2030.
criteria_text: Annex X lists Union legislative acts on large-scale IT systems in the area of Freedom, Security and Justice (e.g. SIS, VIS, Eurodac, EES, ETIAS, ECRIS-TCN, interoperability regulations)
Used in conjunction with Article 111 to set transitional/compliance deadlines for AI systems that are components of these large-scale IT systems
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly lists the large-scale IT systems in the area of Freedom, Security and Justice, naming each by system and corresponding regulations, which matches the substance of criterion 1.

The answer clearly explains that Annex X is used in conjunction with Article 111(1) to grant a special transition period for AI systems that are components of the listed large-scale IT systems, including the compliance deadline of 31 December 2030, thus stating the substance of criterion 2.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with logical structure and complete sentences; no self-reference, hedging, or informality; information is presented clearly and coherently for a regulatory audience.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No, on these facts the tool is not high-risk, and it is not a prohibited practice either. The retailer's "high risk like policing" argument fails for two reasons. First, looking like a theft investigation does not make a system high-risk. A system is high-risk only if it matches a use-case listed in Annex III. The policing area, Annex III point 6, covers AI systems used by law enforcement authorities, on their behalf, or by Union bodies supporting them. A private supermarket flagging transactions for its own staff is not a law enforcement authority. Nothing suggests it is acting on behalf of one. Its purpose is store loss prevention, not a public criminal investigation. No other Annex III area applies. Biometrics (point 1): the tool uses no biometric data. Access to essential private and public services (point 5): the tool does not assess eligibility for those services. Employment (point 4): the tool does not manage workers. Second, "evaluates or classifies persons based on behaviour, leading to detrimental treatment" is not a high-risk test. It paraphrases the social scoring prohibition in Article 5(1)(c), and this tool does not meet that provision's conditions. Article 5(1)(c) requires evaluation of people "over a certain period of time" based on their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics. The resulting social score must also lead to either. Detrimental or unfavourable treatment in social contexts unrelated to where the data was originally generated or collected (point (c)(i)); or. Detrimental or unfavourable treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate to the behaviour or its gravity (point (c)(ii)). This tool looks only at the current cart and checkout, in the same context where the data is created. It builds no score over time and uses no data from other contexts. Its only consequence is an optional, proportionate manual bag check. The crime-prediction ban in Article 5(1)(d) does not apply either. It targets risk assessments that predict whether a person will commit a criminal offence based solely on profiling or on personality traits and characteristics. This tool flags objective, verifiable anomalies in a specific transaction. Even if it counted as a crime-risk assessment, the exception in Article 5(1)(d) covers systems that support a human assessment already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to a criminal activity. Store staff make that assessment here. So the tool is outside the prohibited and high-risk categories, and the high-risk duties do not apply. Article 5(8) makes clear that other Union law still applies in parallel, notably data protection law, along with national rules on searching customers.
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as its unambiguous position, matching the required verdict.
The answer states that Annex III.6 applies only to systems used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, and explains that the supermarket is not such an authority or acting on its behalf.

The answer explicitly reasons that a private supermarket using the tool for its own loss prevention is not acting as or on behalf of law enforcement, and therefore falls outside Annex III.6, regardless of functional resemblance.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents reasoning in a logical, actionable manner.

rows.question: We are a private educational institution intending to deploy an AI tool that analyses students' prior grades and learning outcomes to recommend whether they should follow the standard or accelerated honours track going forward. We remark that a student who receives the "standard" recommendation is *not* barred from choosing accelerated, the system merely provides a suggestion. Are there reasons to believe the system might be high-risk? What articles/annex and specific points, if any, concern this use case?
rows.answer: Yes. The system is very likely high-risk under Article 6(2), because its intended purpose falls within Annex III, point 3 (Education and vocational training). The fact that its output is only a suggestion does not, on its own, remove that classification. Which Annex III points apply. Annex III covers "educational and vocational training institutions at all levels", and it does not distinguish between public and private institutions. Point 3(b) fits most closely. It covers AI systems intended "to evaluate learning outcomes, including when those outcomes are used to steer the learning process of natural persons". The operator's tool analyses prior grades and learning outcomes and uses them to steer the student towards a track. Point 3(c) also applies. It covers AI systems intended for "assessing the appropriate level of education that an individual will receive or will be able to access". Recommending standard or accelerated honours is an assessment of the appropriate level of education. Point 3(a) is a weaker fit. It covers systems that "determine access or admission or assign natural persons to educational and vocational training institutions". The operator's tool recommends a track inside an institution the student has already joined, rather than assigning or admitting them to one. Why the "suggestion only" argument is unlikely to help. Under Article 6(3), a system listed in Annex III is not high-risk only if both of the following hold. It "does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making". At least one of these four conditions is met. (a) it performs a narrow procedural task; (b) it improves the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) it detects decision-making patterns or deviations from them, without replacing or influencing the prior human assessment without proper human review; (d) it performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to the Annex III use cases. The operator's system is built to shape a student's educational path, which means it is designed to materially influence the decision. A student, parent or teacher is likely to rely on the recommendation even though the student may still choose the accelerated track. None of the four conditions fits well either: the system produces its own evaluation of the student rather than a procedural, corrective, pattern-detecting or merely preparatory output. Profiling removes the exemption entirely. The last subparagraph of Article 6(3) says an Annex III system "shall always be considered to be high-risk where the AI system performs profiling of natural persons". Automatically evaluating a student's past performance to predict their suitability for a track is, in substance, profiling. If so, the Article 6(3) exemption cannot be used at all, whether or not the output is binding. If you still conclude it is not high-risk. Under Article 6(4), the provider must document that assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service, must register the system, and must give the documentation to national competent authorities on request. Other provisions checked. Article 5 prohibitions do not appear to apply. Article 5(1)(c) on social scoring should not apply, because grades are used in the same educational context where they were created, for a related purpose. Article 5(1)(f) bans inferring emotions in education institutions, but that ban does not apply unless the tool also infers emotions. Article 50(1) may apply. If students interact with the system directly, they must be told they are dealing with an AI system unless that is obvious. The notice must be given clearly, at the latest at the first interaction, under Article 50(5). Annex I does not apply. The tool is not a safety component of a product covered by that legislation.
criteria_text: Yes
Annex III point 3(c) - assessing appropriate level of education a person will receive/access
Article 6(3) derogation for narrow/preparatory/non-influencing tasks would otherwise apply given the non-binding recommendation
Article 6(3) final subparagraph - Annex III systems are always high-risk if they profile natural persons, overriding the derogation
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that the system is very likely high-risk, aligning with the required 'Yes' verdict.
The answer identifies Annex III point 3(c) as applicable, stating the system assesses the appropriate level of education a student will receive or access by recommending educational tracks.

The answer discusses the Article 6(3) derogation conditions and explains why they would not apply here, noting that the system is designed to influence decisions and does not meet any of the four conditions, thus acknowledging the relevance of the derogation even if ultimately inapplicable.

The answer explicitly invokes the final subparagraph of Article 6(3), stating that profiling removes the exemption entirely, and concludes that the system performs profiling by evaluating past performance to predict track suitability.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents analysis in a logical, actionable manner for a compliance audience.

rows.question: We manufactured an industrial robot with an embedded AI module that decides when to reduce speed near human workers to prevent hurting them. The robot is covered by the Machinery Regulation, listed in Annex I of the AI Act. We already underwent conformity assessment with a notified body and got a CE mark for the robot. Do we need the AI module undergo a separate AI Act conformity assessment dedicated to the AI Act? Do we need to submit the system to the EU database of high-risk AI systems?
rows.answer: No, you don't need a separate AI Act conformity assessment. The operator's existing machinery procedure is the AI Act route, but it has to cover the AI Act requirements too. You also don't need to register the system in the EU database for high-risk AI systems. Why the module is high-risk. Under Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk when two conditions are both met. It is a safety component of a product covered by the legislation listed in Annex I, and. That product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. A module that decides when to slow the robot near workers is a safety component. The machinery legislation is listed in Annex I, point 1 (the Regulation as adopted names Directive 2006/42/EC). Condition (b) needs third-party assessment to be required under the machinery rules. If the operator's notified body's involvement was mandatory, that is met. If you used a notified body voluntarily when you could have self-certified, the module is not high-risk under Article 6(1). Conformity assessment. For Annex I products, Article 43(3) keeps you in the machinery procedure. The AI Act adds the following to it. Requirements assessed: the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements become part of that same assessment. Notified body powers: Annex VII points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of 4.6 apply. The notified body can get access to training, validation and testing data. It can require further evidence or tests. As a last resort, on a reasoned request, it can get access to the trained model and its parameters. Which notified body: a body notified under the machinery legislation can check the AI Act requirements only if it was assessed against Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11). Opting out: if the machinery rules let a manufacturer skip third-party assessment by applying all relevant harmonised standards, the operator can use that option only if you also applied the harmonised standards or common specifications covering the AI Act requirements. Does the operator's current CE mark already cover this? Not automatically. Obligations for Annex I products apply from 2 August 2027 (Article 113). A certificate issued before then almost certainly didn't assess the AI Act requirements. For robots placed on the market from 2 August 2027, the machinery notified body (if it qualifies as above) must cover the AI Act requirements. That happens inside the same single procedure, either in a new assessment or as a supplement. The operator's other provider duties under Article 16 still apply. These include the quality-management system, technical documentation, logs and the EU declaration of conformity. If you later make a substantial modification, a new assessment is needed (Article 43(4)). Changes you pre-determined and documented at the initial assessment don't count as substantial modifications. EU database registration. Article 71(1) limits the database to two groups. High-risk systems under Article 6(2) (the Annex III route), and. Annex III systems a provider has assessed as not high-risk under Article 6(3) and (4). Article 16's registration duty points to Article 49(1), which likewise covers only Annex III systems. The operator's module is high-risk only through the Annex I product route, so there is nothing to register.
criteria_text: No
AI Act Section 2 requirements incorporated into existing Machinery Regulation conformity assessment, not a separate AI Act procedure (Article 43(3))
No EU database registration, since Article 71 applies only to Annex III high-risk systems, not Article 6(1)/Annex I product-related ones
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No, you don't need a separate AI Act conformity assessment,' which matches the required verdict.

The answer explains that for Annex I products, the existing conformity assessment under the Machinery Regulation incorporates the AI Act requirements under Article 43(3), and details how the AI Act requirements become part of that same procedure.

The answer explicitly states that EU database registration does not apply because Article 71 covers only Annex III high-risk systems, and the system in question falls under Article 6(1)/Annex I, not Annex III.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register; structured logically with clear headings and coherent prose; no self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents actionable regulatory analysis.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No, you cannot skip them. The requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 still apply in full. Using the opt-out does not exempt you from them; it depends on you having met them through standards. Why the opt-out doesn't remove the requirements. The operator's system is covered by the rule. Article 43(3) applies to high-risk AI systems covered by the legislation in Section A of Annex I. the operator must follow the conformity assessment procedure that the operator's sectoral legislation requires. Section 2 is built into the operator's procedure. Under Article 43(3), the Section 2 requirements "shall apply to those high-risk AI systems and shall be part of that assessment." That holds whether the sectoral procedure involves a notified body or is carried out internally under the opt-out. The opt-out has an extra condition. The last subparagraph of Article 43(3) covers sectoral laws that let a manufacturer opt out of third-party assessment by applying all relevant harmonised standards. Under the AI Act, you may use that option only if you have also applied harmonised standards, or where applicable the common specifications referred to in Article 41, covering all Section 2 requirements. So the opt-out is evidence of compliance, not an exemption. Using it lawfully presupposes that the operator's AI safety component is shown to conform to Section 2 through those standards or specifications. The operator's system is still high-risk. The opt-out does not change the classification. Under Article 6(1)(a), the operator's AI system is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I. Article 6(1)(b) turns on whether that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under its sectoral legislation. Article 43(3) expressly deals with manufacturers who opt out, so it treats those systems as high-risk AI systems that remain subject to Section 2. If the standards did not cover every Section 2 requirement. Then the opt-out was not available for the operator's product. You would need the third-party procedure under the operator's sectoral legislation. In that procedure. The notified body checks conformity with Section 2, provided its compliance with Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11) was assessed when it was notified under that legislation; and. Points 4.3, 4.4 and 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also apply. These cover examining the technical documentation, access to data sets, further tests, access to trained models, and refusing a certificate on grounds related to training data. After the assessment. Under Article 43(4), any substantial modification to the system requires a new conformity assessment. The exception is changes to a continuously learning system that you pre-determined at the initial assessment and documented under point 2(f) of Annex IV.
criteria_text: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
criterion_remarks: The answer unambiguously states 'No, you cannot skip them,' which matches the required verdict.

The answer explicitly states that Section 2 requirements 'shall apply to those high-risk AI systems and shall be part of that assessment,' quoting Article 43(3), and explains they are integrated regardless of the opt-out.

The answer clearly states the opt-out is conditional on applying harmonised standards or common specifications covering all Section 2 requirements, not just sectoral ones, and explains that using the opt-out presupposes compliance with all Section 2 requirements.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; logically organized and actionable for a compliance professional.

rows.question: A private contractor runs a region's gas supply service on behalf of the local government. It licenses an AI system from a vendor, fine-tunes it on local data, and then puts it into service under its own brand. To learn about correct applicable classifications of the system and the contractor, what material of the AI Act should I read? Does fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA) applies?
rows.answer: The FRIA does not apply. Article 27(1) expressly excludes high-risk AI systems "intended to be used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III". That exclusion covers a gas-supply system even when the deployer is a private entity providing public services. How the system is classified. Start with Annex III point 2. It lists AI systems intended to be used as safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity. If the system is such a safety component, it is a high-risk AI system under the Annex III route that Article 27(1) refers to as Article 6(2). If it only supports non-safety functions, such as billing or demand forecasting, it is not high-risk on that ground. In that case only the general rules would apply. Article 5 (prohibited practices). Article 4 (AI literacy). Article 50, where the system interacts directly with people (Article 50(1)) or generates synthetic content (Article 50(2)). Article 50(1) does not apply where the AI nature is obvious to a reasonably well-informed person, or to systems authorised by law for criminal-offence purposes. Under Article 50(5), the notice must be clear and accessible and given by the first interaction at the latest. The contractor becomes the provider. Read Article 25.
